Container scheduling.title: Deep Reinforcement Learning for Multi-UAV Data Harvesting Under Variable Team Sizes and Agent Loss
Container scheduling.summary: Collecting data from wireless sensors can be challenging when limited communication infrastructure prevents them from offloading their measurements. In such settings, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) can exploit their mobility to harvest data locally, while coordinated UAV teams can provide efficient and redundant coverage of remote areas. Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) enables such teams to learn decentralized coordination policies. However, training separate policies for different team and sensor populations is costly, and fixed-population policies may be vulnerable to agent failures. This work proposes F-MADDPG, a flexible variant of Multi-Agent Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (MADDPG) that supports data harvesting with varying numbers of wireless sensors and UAVs. The framework also accommodates unexpected catastrophic failures that permanently remove agents during a mission. We compare F-MADDPG with a MADDPG baseline that uses multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) and evaluate training strategies based on team-size sampling and exposure to agent terminations. The results show that F-MADDPG learns across the evaluated population sizes, completes missions faster than the baseline on average, benefits from inverse-cardinality team-size sampling compared with uniform sampling, remains effective after permanent agent losses, and gains no consistent benefit from exposure to failures during training.

Container scheduling.title: Large-Scale Gaussian Splatting with a Multi-GPU PyTorch Backend
Container scheduling.summary: Gaussian splatting methods have become increasingly popular for neural reconstruction of the real world. However, they are often limited in scale and resolution due to compute and memory constraints. We present a multi-GPU Gaussian splatting approach that scales reconstruction to higher resolutions and larger scenes while abstracting away the code complexity typically associated with distributing a model. We demonstrate city-scale reconstructions with street-level detail consisting of over 1 billion Gaussian splats. To accomplish this, we propose a PyTorch backend that distributes parameters and operators across GPUs via CUDA unified memory, with optional NVLink support. Because distribution occurs at the operator level, the model code requires no explicit cross-device communication. More broadly, the backend exposes multiple GPUs as an aggregate asynchronous PyTorch device and supports a broad set of PyTorch operators enabling the distribution of general PyTorch workloads.
Container scheduling.comment: 13 pages, 8 tables, 4 figures, and 1 listing. Includes supplementary material

Container scheduling.title: Ostinato: Low-Latency CPU-GPU MoE Inference for Local Agents
Container scheduling.summary: Language-model agents increasingly run on local workstations with consumer GPUs, where quantized mixture-of-experts (MoE) models split routed experts between GPU and host memory. Prefix-cached agent sessions alternate single-token decode with short tool-return prefills, typically up to a few hundred tokens. Short tool turns touch more experts than consumer GPUs can hold, yet direct roughly 85% of DeepSeek-V4-Flash's routes to a static GPU pool while leaving 3.3-5.5 tokens per cold expert. Widely used local engines such as llama.cpp and KTransformers either copy tens of gigabytes over PCIe per turn, compute every route on the CPU while idling resident GPU experts, or budget GPU memory by whole layers and uniform per-layer quotas. We present Ostinato, a CPU-GPU MoE engine that reuses one static cross-layer GPU pool in place across every forward pass. During decode and short tool turns, Ostinato computes resident routes on the GPUs and sparse cold routes on the CPU, so short turns copy no expert weights; on long prefills, it deduplicates cold uploads; and for multi-GPU decode, all-zero expert slots with device-side synchronization capture each GPU's decode step in one CUDA graph. Across held-out SWE and -bench sessions on three MoE models, Ostinato cuts median tool-turn waits by 2.5-6.6x and finishes sessions 1.36-3.83x faster than default baselines, staying 1.30-1.94x faster when baselines align their upload threshold and weight loading. It finishes sessions fastest across seven agent workloads, one to four GPUs, and up to eight concurrent sessions, while its cross-layer pool speeds up 335 GB DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash by 1.81-2.19x over llama.cpp's expert cache.

Container scheduling.title: PipeAxes: Decoupling Compute and Communication Granularities for Pipeline-Parallel LLM Serving
Container scheduling.summary:
Pipeline parallelism can serve long-context language models on PCIe servers and across heterogeneous GPU clusters. Existing engines split prefill into token chunks to limit decode stalls. The chunk size also sets the GPU batch width and the size of activation transfers between stages. Small chunks reload model weights more often. Large chunks can keep the GPU and the link busy long enough to delay interactive requests.
  PipeAxes runs wide prefill batches a few layers at a time so decodes can run between slices. A fused Triton Hadamard-INT4 codec compresses activations, which travel in independently sized row groups over parallel TCP sockets. The scheduler uses latency slack to choose batch width, slice depth, and row-group size. We evaluated PipeAxes in 97 replays covering 5,016 requests on A800, RTX 4090, and RTX 3090 GPUs. All 74 requests met their latency targets during a tenfold bandwidth swing. In a four-stage mixture-of-experts pipeline, PipeAxes served requests within their latency targets at 23.3x the rate of calibrated Revisit-PP and 4.44x the rate of Fixed-4096 with Express. In a mixed 64K-context workload, p95 time to first token for short requests fell from 129.8 s with native vLLM to 512 ms. With INT4 transport, MMLU accuracy rose by 0.06 percentage points and GSM8K accuracy fell by 0.46 percentage points relative to BF16.

Container scheduling.title: Reducing Fixed-Batch Client Idleness in Many-Client Edge Split Learning
Container scheduling.summary: Parallel Split Learning with Global Sampling (GPSL) trains a split model on a fixed-size batch drawn from the data of all clients. When the client population is much larger than the batch, most clients contribute no data in a round, and additional server capacity does not change this. We propose Global Clustered Parallel Split Learning (GCPSL), which assigns clients to stable clusters, runs one GPSL workload per cluster concurrently, and periodically fuses the split-model replicas. We derive the expected direct data participation under the batch sampler, which separates repeated sampling of the same clients from idling at the fusion barrier. With 256 clients, more clusters raise participation but reduce the client diversity seen by each workload. In three paired runs on four H100 GPUs, GCPSL raises direct data participation from 22% to 57-60%. With random or size-balanced clusters, it reaches 85% CIFAR-10 validation accuracy in 5.7 minutes, 1.6 times faster than GPSL with its batch sharded across the same GPUs. It matches per-step synchronized data-parallel GPSL at 85% and reaches 88% in about 10 instead of 19.5 minutes, without per-step global gradient or BatchNorm synchronization. Concurrent execution is 3.11 times faster than sequential execution of the same workloads.
Container scheduling.comment: 12 pages, 6 figures, 7 tables. Extended version of v1 under a new title, with two additional authors. Corrects the accuracy values and target rounds of the schedule-accounted CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 studies: v1 reported a batch-averaged macro accuracy. The real-execution measurements are unchanged

Container scheduling.title: DéjàVu: Plurality Consensus by First Repetition
Container scheduling.summary:
We analyze DéjàVu, a simple protocol for plurality consensus: in each synchronous round, each agent samples one uniformly random agent and adopts the first opinion it observes twice, resetting its memory after every adoption. The rule requires neither frequency counters nor knowledge of the population size or the number of opinions. It relies only on repetition detection, an ability documented in single neurons and reflected in the mere-exposure effect.
  For a population of $n$ agents with $k$ initial opinions, let $M_0$ be the initial count of the plurality opinion (so $n/M_0 \le k$) and $Δ_0$ its bias, the difference between $M_0$ and the count of the second most popular opinion. We prove that, whenever $Δ_0 = Ω(\sqrt{M_0 \log n})$, DéjàVu reaches consensus on the initial plurality opinion within $O(\sqrt{n/M_0} \log(e M_0 / Δ_0) + \log\log n)$ rounds with high probability. Moreover, we show that, for the same bias regime, DéjàVu is asymptotically never slower than the $h$-majority protocol, collecting its $h$ samples one per round, for every fixed choice of $h$, even one chosen optimally for the initial configuration. There are also initial configurations for which DéjàVu is asymptotically faster for every $h$.
  The opinion counts alone do not determine the dynamics: each adoption depends on a hidden memory filled over many rounds while the population changed, and agents with older (hence fuller) memories tend to reset sooner, so an advantage held mostly by them can be lost. The few rigorous convergence results we are aware of for such dynamics concern only two opinions. We derive the exact law of the memories given the history of opinions and resets, and track how the plurality opinion's advantage is distributed across memory ages, giving more weight to recently reset agents as they are less likely to reset again soon.

Container scheduling.title: High-performance metapopulation models for epidemic emergencies: Scalability and performance of implicit and explicit mobility representations on CPUs and GPUs
Container scheduling.summary: Epidemics form a subclass of natural disasters impacting countries or entire continents, where suitable reactions might differ substantially across spatio-temporal dimensions. Spatially resolved models based on ordinary differential equations (ODEs) are an efficient modeling approach for large and distributed populations. Commonly referred to as metapopulation models, they allow a realistic representation of spatial heterogeneities and mobility. Yet, their application in epidemic settings under high time pressure requires efficient, parallelized implementations leveraging modern supercomputers. The different ways to represent mobility in metapopulation models affect both epidemic trajectories and computational costs. In contrast to implicit mobility modeling, where populations are coupled through transition and transmission intensities, explicit Lagrangian mobility tracks traveling subpopulations according to their home and current location. In this paper, we compare metapopulation models with implicit and explicit mobility. A four-patch experiment shows that the trajectories of both formulations remain close, but differences increase with the mobility cycle length. We present CPU- and GPU-based parallelizations and analyze fully connected networks with up to 16,384 patches on 128 CPU cores and NVIDIA A100 and H100 GPUs. Roofline analyses show near-maximum performance for the most time-consuming GPU subroutines and identify data reuse and the cost of mobility events as the main performance drivers. Our results show that mobility assumptions, event frequency, numerical solvers, and available hardware need to be considered together when developing metapopulation models for epidemic emergencies. In a synthesized setting with a disease outbreak in central Europe, we show how a worldwide pandemic with 12,865 patches and four billion state variables can be simulated in 24 seconds using GPUs.

Container scheduling.title: Same Seed, Different Top Prediction: Cross-Platform Reproducibility of AlphaFold 3 Inference on TPUs, GPUs, and CPUs
Container scheduling.summary: AlphaFold 3 returns the highest-ranked of several sampled structures and computes each prediction on one device. Computing centers may schedule them on different GPU types or CPU nodes. Floating-point results can differ between devices, so the same input and seed may return another structure. Neither AlphaFold 3's documentation nor its outputs warn of this. We measure how often the device changes the returned structure, and tell users what to report and how to make devices agree. We used identical inputs, weights, seeds, and settings on two Google tensor processing unit (TPU) generations (v5e, v6e), three NVIDIA GPUs (L4, A100, H100), and an Intel Xeon CPU. On 60 protein-ligand complexes, with five seeds each, switching TPU generations changed the top-ranked sample in 18.0% of 300 predictions. Recompiling never changed it on either TPU, but did so in 7.3% on the L4 GPU. Yet the structures barely moved. The top-ranked pose switched between correct and incorrect in 3.3% to 3.7% of predictions, against about 10% for a new seed. These switches nearly always came from one validity check, with the ligand within 2 angstroms. Follow-ups found the effect again on 72 new targets and between the TPUs and the CPU. Between the A100 and H100 it exceeded recompilation, although AlphaFold 3's developers verified its numerical accuracy on both. An exploratory analysis links the changes to near-tied candidates. We recommend reporting the device and every near-tied sample. A float32 trunk with full-precision matrix products made all five accelerators agree on nearly every prediction.
Container scheduling.comment: 102 pages: 14 pages of paper (4 figures, 6 tables) and 88 pages of supplementary material. Code: https://github.com/lorenzopazienza/af3-cross-platform. Data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24057470 and https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24057544. Pre-registration: https://osf.io/fegsy

Container scheduling.title: Protecting Confidentiality, Privacy and Integrity in Collaborative Learning
Container scheduling.summary:
A collaboration between dataset owners and model owners is needed for effective machine learning (ML) training. During this collaboration, however, dataset owners and model owners want to protect the confidentiality of their respective assets (i.e., datasets, models and training code), with the dataset owners also caring about the privacy of individual users whose data is in the datasets. Existing solutions provide limited confidentiality for models and training code, suffer from data privacy issues, or incur unacceptable performance.
  We present Citadel++, a collaborative ML training system to simultaneously protect the confidentiality of datasets, models and training code as well as the privacy of individual user data. Specifically, Citadel++ takes a chained approach. First, we employ the Virtual Machine-level Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) as the training runtime to provide confidentiality protections for datasets, model and training code. Second, we create a privacy barrier that improves upon differential privacy techniques to safeguard the privacy of individual user data while maintaining model utility. Third, we construct and optimize a Virtual Machine Privilege Level (VMPL)-enforced fine-grained sandbox to regulate the dataflow in the system to ensure that our privacy barrier is always applied even when the model and training code maybe maliciously designed. Finally, we employ specific TEE capabilities to ensure the integrity of our privacy barrier and sandboxing mechanisms for their correct execution.
  To our knowledge, Citadel++ is the first collaborative training system providing strong confidentiality and privacy protections for dataset owners and model owners simultaneously. We analyze Citadel++ security properties and implement a full prototype. Our evaluation shows that Citadel++ provides strong guarantees with modest overheads.

Container scheduling.title: Libtt: A Compiler and Runtime for Tenstorrent Processors
Container scheduling.summary: Libtt brings the PyTorch and JAX ecosystem to Tenstorrent hardware. It implements PJRT, the interface through which XLA-based frameworks drive Google's TPUs, so JAX runs on it directly, PyTorch runs through TorchTPU, and software written for TPUs carries over with no changes except replacing custom kernels. Built on Tenstorrent's open-source compiler and runtime, libtt ships the entire stack, from the compiler to the multi-chip runtime, as a single shared library. It contains extensive fixes to the upstream Tenstorrent software to make existing PyTorch and JAX code work out of the box, and extensive new compiler optimizations to make it fast. It passes most of the JAX and TorchTPU test suites and runs SGLang, TorchTitan, and Miles, covering serving, fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning.

Container scheduling.title: VibeServe: Can AI Agents Build Bespoke LLM Serving Systems?
Container scheduling.summary: For years, we have built LLM serving systems like any other critical infrastructure, with a single general-purpose stack hand-tuned over many engineer-years to support every model and workload. In this paper, we instead let coding agents build bespoke serving systems for different usage scenarios. We propose VibeServe, the first agentic loop that generates entire LLM serving stacks end-to-end. VibeServe uses an outer loop to plan and track the search over system designs, and an inner loop to implement candidates, check correctness, and measure performance on the target benchmark. In standard serving settings, VibeServe matches vLLM and SGLang on Llama-3.1-8B, and delivers 2.3x the goodput of a tuned SGLang for a 397B MoE model on four AMD MI300As. In five non-standard scenarios, VibeServe outperforms existing systems by exploiting opportunities that generic systems miss, spanning non-standard model architectures, workload knowledge, and hardware-specific optimizations. Together, these results show that coding agents can construct and specialize competitive serving systems across heterogeneous deployment targets. Code is available at https://github.com/uw-syfi/vibesys.

Container scheduling.title: A Local-Counting Approach for Distributed Induced Path Detection
Container scheduling.summary:
A well-known application of the celebrated color-coding technique is fast detection of paths in a distributed setting with limited bandwidth, by propagating a signal along colorful paths [Even et al., DISC 2017]. However, since vertices of the same color are indistinguishable by this procedure, it cannot detect induced paths, as they appear the same as cycles.
  We make the following observation. If, for a given edge, we \emph{count} the number of such signals over all permutations of the random coloring that terminate at that edge, then we can separate an induced path from a cycle: an induced path contributes one to that count, while a cycle contributes two. Refining and generalizing this observation gives our \emph{local-counting approach}, which allows us to separate induced paths from any other subgraph.
  We establish the following end results, all improving upon the state of the art in their round complexities and refined detection variants.
  * An $O(1)$-round algorithm for induced $P_4$ detection.
  * $O(Δ)$-round algorithms for detection of induced $P_5$ and $P_6$.
  * An $\tilde{O}(n^{1/3})$-round algorithm for detection of induced $P_5$ in induced-$C_4$ free graphs.

Container scheduling.title: CoordRoute: Coordinated Multi-Model Routing for Maximum Compute-Budget Utility
Container scheduling.summary: Model routing sends each request to one of several large language models (LLMs) of different sizes. In practice, requests share a fixed compute budget: a spending cap on rented model APIs or the capacity of a private GPU cluster. Most existing routers do not account for the total budget: each decides a request on its own, so per-request optima are not optimal overall. We advocate coordinated routing, which allocates the budget across requests to maximize its utility, their total satisfaction, along a predict-plan-rectify route: predict what each model would give and cost, plan the choice against later requests, and rectify it during generation. Each step faces a challenge: a request's gain from each model is uncertain before generation, later arrivals are unknown when a request must start, and observing answers during generation consumes the budget itself. CoordRoute addresses them with relative demand prediction, which compares candidate models through past requests that lead to the same routing choices; a lookahead solver, which charges each choice for what its compute could earn for later requests; and budget-aware runtime correction, which drops or upgrades in-flight requests at the same price, inspecting answers only when it pays off. On Azure Conversation and BurstGPT traces, CoordRoute improves total satisfaction by 18.72% over the strongest existing router.

Container scheduling.title: CompileMask: Bridging the Gap Between Expressiveness and Efficiency in Attention Masking
Container scheduling.summary: Modern attention workloads require diverse masks whose shapes depend on per-sequence parameters, yet efficient attention kernels natively support only a small set of mask patterns. Existing methods for custom masks face an expressiveness-efficiency trade-off. Predicate-based methods are expressive but evaluate a user-defined predicate on every element at substantial cost, whereas interval-based methods execute efficiently but lack the expressiveness for complex masks. We present CompileMask, which bridges this gap by compiling the mask predicate users write into an Execution Descriptor that the attention kernel executes efficiently. We design a compiler that automatically lowers a mask predicate into an intermediate representation and generates a mask-specific preprocessing kernel, which builds the descriptor for each batch with a few expressions per row rather than by evaluating the predicate on every element. We further propose Tile-local Records, a compact representation of row visibility within each tile that lets the attention kernel check every element with a few integer operations, so that masking stays efficient even for complex masks. Experiments show that CompileMask achieves up to $3.3\times$ speedup over FlexAttention and up to $1.2\times$ over FlashMask in single-operator benchmarks, while supporting complex masks that FlashMask cannot express.

Container scheduling.title: Beyond Hotness: High-Resolution Memory Characterization of Cloud and LLM Workloads for Tiered Memory with ARM SPE
Container scheduling.summary: Memory demands from data analytics and LLM workloads grow rapidly, driving up memory costs in cloud and data centers. Multi-tier memory has emerged as a promising solution to balance performance and cost. However, effectively leveraging it requires a deep understanding of workload memory behaviors. This work introduces a high-resolution memory characterization methodology for analyzing workload-specific opportunities for multi-tier memory usage. In response to the increasing deployment of ARM-based processors in data centers, we implement our methodology using the recent Statistical Profiling Extension (SPE) for ARM. By characterizing eight memory-intensive workloads from CloudSuite and LLM applications, we identify region-specific access patterns, evaluate the effectiveness of cloud-oriented cache hierarchies, and propose new metrics based on memory idle periods and latency profiles to determine suitable data placement for tiered memory.

Container scheduling.title: Asymmetric Speculative Decoding: Unlocking In-Context Learning in Draft Models
Container scheduling.summary: Speculative decoding addresses Large Language Model (LLM) inference latency by first drafting and then verifying in parallel. Yet practical speedups fall far short of theoretical bounds, especially on reasoning tasks. We identify the root cause as task isomorphism: existing methods provide identical prompts to both models, forcing the draft model to solve problems beyond its capacity. This produces high rejection rates that eliminate parallelization gains. We discover that acceptance rates increase monotonically during generation, revealing a latent in-context learning (ICL) effect wherein the draft model progressively aligns with the target distribution by learning from verified tokens. Controlled experiments with varying context window sizes confirm this improvement stems from ICL-driven alignment rather than token difficulty. Motivated by this finding, we propose Asymmetric Speculative Decoding (AsymSpec), a training-free framework that decouples the prompts provided to draft and target models. By supplying the draft model with task-relevant example solutions, we reformulate its objective from reasoning to simulation, amplifying the ICL effect from the first token. We prove AsymSpec produces exact samples and converges exponentially to the target distribution. Across reasoning, code generation, and summarization tasks, AsymSpec achieves 2.29$\times$ to 4.95$\times$ speedup over autoregressive decoding, outperforming standard speculative decoding without model retraining.

Container scheduling.title: Privacy-Aware Adaptive Client Selection for Federated Retrieval-Augmented Generation
Container scheduling.summary: Federated retrieval-augmented generation retrieves evidence from distributed corpora. However, broadcasting queries to all clients increases the retrieval burden and query exposure. We present Privacy-Aware Adaptive Client Selection for Federated Retrieval-Augmented Generation (PACS-FedRAG), an online selector that takes into account perturbed semantic profiles along with evidence feedback, latency, payload cost, and exploration. In a ten-client setting where three clients are chosen, the archived end-to-end benchmark reports an evidence overlap of 0.372 and an answer accuracy of 0.287. The retrieval-only evaluation, on the other hand, reuses a full-broadcast baseline with a different fusion tie-breaking policy. Rank fusion across disjoint client corpora imposes an overlap ceiling of 0.375, limiting its interpretation as a relevance measure. Answer accuracy is below the fixed-label diagnostic of 0.645, and raw generator responses are unavailable for parser verification. Corrected baselines and a new answer-level evaluation are needed to assess whether quality is preserved. Selecting three clients reduces the number of query recipients by 70%. Profile perturbation does not provide confidentiality of queries or passages.

Container scheduling.title: VoroPlex: A Python Framework for Multi-Threaded and Differentiable Voronoi Tessellation
Container scheduling.summary: Voronoi tessellations are widely used in computational physics, for example to measure local structure in particle systems and to generate meshes. We present VoroPlex, an open-source Python package for computing Voronoi tessellations in two and three dimensions. VoroPlex is built on the multi-threaded version of the C++ library Voro++, so that large tessellations can be computed in parallel. The package also makes the tessellation differentiable. Each Voronoi vertex is labeled by the generators that define it, and VoroPlex uses these labels to compute the derivative of the vertex with respect to the positions of these generators. PyTorch can therefore compute gradients of quantities such as cell areas, volumes, and interface areas with respect to the generator positions, so that these quantities can be optimized using standard gradient-based methods. The package also includes tools for extracting interfaces between groups of cells and for exporting meshes. For one million points using 28 threads, VoroPlex is 46 times faster than SciPy in 2D and 39 times faster in 3D. We demonstrate the package with three applications: centroidal Voronoi tessellations with a variable density, meshing of 2D shapes defined by signed distance functions, and the design of foams with a preferred cell orientation.

Container scheduling.title: MEV-ACE: Identity-Authenticated Fair Ordering for Proposer-Controlled MEV Mitigation
Container scheduling.summary: Maximal Extractable Value, or MEV, remains a structural threat to blockchain fairness because a block producer can often observe pending transactions and unilaterally decide their ordering or inclusion. Existing mitigations hide transaction contents or outsource ordering, but they often leave two gaps unresolved. First, commitments are not authenticated by slashable identities. Second, inclusion obligations are not backed by transferable evidence that other validators can verify. This paper presents MEV ACE, a fair ordering protocol for proposer controlled ordering MEV. MEV ACE combines three mechanisms. First, it uses registered economic identities whose authentication keys are deterministically derived from the ACE GF framework and bonded on chain. Second, it uses authenticated commit and open messages with validator receipt thresholds, which make admissibility and inclusion obligations independently auditable. Third, it uses verifiable delay based randomness to determine transaction order only after the admissible commitment set is fixed. We formalize the protocol in a Byzantine fault tolerant validator model with threshold receipts and show three properties under standard assumptions: order unpredictability after the admissible set is locked, commitment authenticity under signature unforgeability, and accountable inclusion for transactions that obtain threshold commit and open receipts. Under these conditions, and when producer and user bonds exceed the one slot gain from invalid execution or selective non opening, MEV ACE removes unilateral proposer discretion over front running, sandwich attacks, and censorship against admitted transactions. The protocol remains single slot in structure, requires no threshold decryption committee, and is compatible with post quantum signature schemes such as ML DSA 44.

Container scheduling.title: HFIPay: Privacy-Preserving, Cross-Chain Cryptocurrency Payments to Human-Friendly Identifiers
Container scheduling.summary: Human-friendly identifiers such as email addresses and phone numbers are convenient payment targets, but direct mappings from identifiers to blockchain addresses make balances and transaction histories enumerable by anyone who knows the identifier. We present HFI-Pay, a relay-assisted protocol for privacy-preserving identifier-routed cryptocurrency payments. The relay resolves the identifier off-chain and registers only a random intent identifier, a per-intent blinded binding rho_i, and the quoted payment tuple on-chain; no identifier or reusable recipient tag is published before claim. In a verified-quote deployment, the sender verifies an attested quote proving that rho_i was derived from the same hidden binding handle as the recipient's attested binding-key commitment, preventing relay-side recipient substitution before funding. Claims are authorized by a zero-knowledge proof, instantiated through ZK-ACE, that the claimant controls the deterministic identity whose epoch-scoped handle opens the blinded binding and authorizes release of the quoted asset and amount to a chosen destination. We define observer-model games for enumeration resistance and pre-claim unlinkability, state the composition needed for post-quote claim correctness, and characterize relay compromise and post-claim linkability. Keywords: identifier-based payment, privacy-preserving, verifiable quote, blinded claim binding, zero-knowledge authorization

Container scheduling.title: n-VM: A Multi-VM Layer-1 Architecture with Shared Identity and Token State
Container scheduling.summary: Multi-chain ecosystems suffer from fragmented identity, siloed liquidity, and bridge-dependent token transfers. We present n-VM, a Layer-1 architecture that hosts n heterogeneous virtual machines as co-equal execution environments over shared consensus and shared state. The design combines three components: a dispatcher that routes transactions by opcode prefix, a unified identity layer in which one 32-byte commitment anchors VM-specifific addresses, and a unified token ledger that exposes VM-native interfaces such as ERC-20 and SPL over a common balance store. We formalize routing, identity derivation, and token transfer semantics, and prove cross-VM transfer atomicity and identity isolation under standard cryptographic assumptions. We describe a concrete instantiation with five VMs: a native runtime, EVM, SVM, Bitcoin Script, and TVM. We also present context-based sharding and a write-set scheduler for parallel execution. Under an analytical throughput model, the architecture admits a projected range of about 16,000 to 66,000 transactions per second on commodity hardware.

Container scheduling.title: ACE Runtime - A ZKP-Native Blockchain Runtime with Sub-Second Cryptographic Finality
Container scheduling.summary: Existing high performance blockchains verify one signature per transaction on the critical path, which creates O(N) verification cost, high hardware pressure, and difficult post quantum migration. This paper presents ACE Runtime, a ZKP native execution layer built on identity authorization separation. We replace per transaction signature checks with lightweight HMAC attestations in the hot path, then generate one aggregated zero knowledge finality certificate per block in an asynchronous prove stage. The system is organized as an Attest Execute Prove pipeline with two tier finality: soft finality from BFT voting and hard finality from proof verification. Under standard cryptographic assumptions, we provide formal arguments for attestation unforgeability and hard finality irreversibility. We also define a two phase timeout and backup proving path with witness availability gossip for liveness under builder failure. Quantitative results combine analytical modeling with reference implementation measurements. The prototype shows low CPU orchestration overhead, while model driven analysis projects constant per block verification cost, lower validator hardware requirements for non builders, and better bandwidth efficiency than per transaction signature designs. These results indicate that identity authorization separation is a practical architecture for sub second cryptographic finality with a clear path toward stronger post quantum components.

Container scheduling.title: ACE-GF-based Attestation Relay for PQC - Lightweight Mempool Propagation Without On-Path Proofs
Container scheduling.summary: In post-quantum blockchain settings, objects that require validity proofs (e.g., blob roots, execution-layer or consensus-layer signature aggregates) must be broadcast through mempool and relay networks. Recursive STARKs have been proposed to aggregate such proofs so that each node forwards one proof per tick plus objects without proofs, capping per-node proof bandwidth at roughly 128 KB degree per tick. We observe that propagation does not inherently require validity proofs on the path-only a lightweight assurance that an object is eligible for relay. We present AR-ACE (ACE-GF-based Attestation Relay for PQC), in which relay nodes forward objects plus compact attestations (e.g., identity-bound signatures or commitments) and do not generate, hold, or forward any full validity proof. Only the builder (or final verifier) performs a single aggregated validity proof over the set of objects it includes. This proof-off-path design removes proof overhead from the propagation path entirely, yielding an order-of-magnitude reduction in proof-related relay bandwidth relative to proof-carrying propagation. When instantiated with ACE-GF-derived attestation keys, AR-ACE preserves a unified identity story with on-chain authorization and is PQC-ready. We specify a protocol model, state design goals and security considerations, define security games, and provide a structural bandwidth comparison with recursive-STARK-based propagation.

Container scheduling.title: ZK-ACE: Identity-Centric Zero-Knowledge Authorization for Post-Quantum Blockchain Systems
Container scheduling.summary:
Post-quantum signature schemes impose kilobyte-scale on-chain artifacts. Verifying them inside ZK circuits merely relocates the cost via expensive lattice arithmetic in prover circuits.
  We present ZK-ACE (Zero-Knowledge Authorization for Cryptographic Entities), which replaces transaction-carried signature objects with identity-bound ZK statements. Given a deterministic identity derivation primitive (DIDP) as a black box, the prover demonstrates in zero knowledge that an identity consistent with an on-chain commitment authorized the transaction; no signature object is produced or verified on-chain.
  We provide game-based definitions and reduction-based proofs for authorization soundness, replay resistance, substitution resistance, and cross-domain separation, under knowledge soundness, collision resistance, and DIDP recovery hardness. Structural data accounting shows an order-of-magnitude reduction in per-transaction authorization data versus direct PQC deployment. A reference implementation offers two backends: Circle STARK (341 active rows / 361 AIR constraint expressions, 14.5 ms prove, 1.1 ms verify, approx. 107 KB proofs, transparent setup, post-quantum-oriented) and Groth16/BN254 (2,155 R1CS constraints, 37.3 ms prove, 128-byte proofs). Both are roughly 500--2,300x smaller than in-circuit PQC signature verification. Under mandatory per-block STARK aggregation, per-transaction consensus-visible data is approx. 160 bytes.

Container scheduling.title: The Bilateral Efficiency of Ethernet: Recalibrating Metcalfe and Boggs After Fifty Years
Container scheduling.summary: In July 1976, Metcalfe and Boggs published their foundational paper on Ethernet in Communications of the ACM. Their efficiency model -- E = (P/C)/(P/C + W*T) -- measures the fraction of Ether time carrying good forward packets under contention. For fifty years this model has framed how the community thinks about Ethernet performance. We argue it is silent on the question that matters for modern intra-rack interconnect: bilateral transaction efficiency -- the fraction of link time that produces committed agreements between sender and receiver. Metcalfe and Boggs themselves planted the seed in their EFTP "end-dally" protocol (Section 7.2.2), and the deeper anchor is older still: Abramson's Alohanet carried positive acknowledgments at the link layer -- a bilateral mechanism Metcalfe consciously removed in 1973 to obtain Ethernet's simple, ACK-free packet format. The result is a fifty-year bilateral zigzag: Aloha (bilateral) to Ethernet (unilateral) to the EFTP end-dally (bilateral) to TCP (unilateral-with-bilateral-above). We formalize bilateral efficiency, connect it to the back-to-back Shannon channel with Perfect Information Feedback, and -- scoping the claim explicitly to intra-rack distances of one meter or less -- describe how the Open Aethernet link recovers mutual knowledge at the link layer. The correction to Table 1 is not a different set of numbers. It is a different question. A new appendix places the 2025-2026 return of link-level retry (UEC, OCP ESUN, UALink) in this history and shows that it restores half of the end-dally: the sender learns of delivery, the receiver never learns that the sender knows. It opens from Ron Crane's observation that produced Fast Ethernet: carried to 100 Gb/s, the same arithmetic makes the minimum frame about one meter long.
Container scheduling.comment: 23 pages, with appendices on the Open Aethernet fault model and the return of link-level retry. 50th anniversary of Metcalfe and Boggs (1976). v4: bilateral efficiency counts committed and complete transactions; Appendix B carries Ron Crane's Fast Ethernet arithmetic to 100 Gb/s and reads the 2025-2026 link-level retry of UEC, ESUN, UALink and IEEE 802 contributions against the end-dally

Some new methods.title: Spectrum Adaptation of AI-Native Autoencoder Communications with Transfer Learning
Some new methods.summary: End-to-end physical-layer learning replaces separate modulation, coding, and detection operations with an autoencoder (AE) that consists of a jointly trained encoder-decoder pair at the transmitter and the receiver. This paper studies AI-native communications with AEs and quantifies the sensitivity to training-test mismatch in channel models. Models trained only on an AWGN channel achieve low bit error rates (BERs) under matched conditions but degrade severely on Rayleigh fading with practical front-end impairments. To reduce the time and energy required to adapt to new channel conditions, we propose a low-latency transfer-learning procedure that starts from an AWGN-pretrained system and fine-tunes only a small subset of transmitter and receiver layers while freezing the remainder. We further formulate layer selection as a budget-constrained optimization problem that identifies the most informative parameters to update during adaptation. This preserves the learned signal geometry and the deep decision structure while adapting lightweight front ends to fading- and impairment-induced mixing. For AE communications, we show that partial updates remove the mismatch-induced error floor and approach the BER of fully retrained models. We provide a layer-wise study and quantify resource-performance trade-offs, showing that modest adaptation substantially reduces BER while cutting training time, multiply-accumulate (MAC) operations, energy consumption, and the fraction of updated parameters for resource-efficient implementation.

Some new methods.title: Attack Policy Selection can Mislead Monitor Evaluators
Some new methods.summary:
AI monitors, classifiers that flag dangerous behaviour by AI agents, are often evaluated against transcripts generated by attack policies acting as proxies for dangerous behaviour in deployment. We evaluate an ex-production OpenAI monitor as a case study and find that measured false negative rate is highly sensitive to both the method used to generate attack policies and the level of optimisation applied within that method. This rate ranged from 0.5\% to 20.8\% across optimisation levels of a single method (reinforcement learning), and from 6.4\% to 23.0\% across methods at their best observed optimisation level (optimised prompting vs.\ transcript editing). Every attack policy was developed against proxy monitors only: all reported results show attacks transferring to the held-out GPT-5.4 target monitor. Our results suggest that monitor evasion evaluations can easily mislead: an evaluation using only basic attack methods may give false confidence that a monitor is strong.
  The sensitivity to attack-policy choice raises a problem: interpreting any particular result as evidence about deployment performance requires justification. The transcripts produced by attack policies are proxies for the dangerous behaviour a monitor must flag in deployment. These proxies can introduce visible artefacts, such as reasoning about a ``side task'' absent from the instructions shown to the monitor, that affect monitor judgements. Given the sensitivity above, the choice of proxy can change an evaluation's conclusion. Reading these results as evidence about deployment therefore requires a separate legitimacy argument for why the proxies are informative, including any justification of conservativeness. Making convincing arguments remains an open problem.

Some new methods.title: Diverse Alternative Reasoning Traces for Hard Math Problems
Some new methods.summary: Post-training large language models (LLMs) for mathematical reasoning often relies on accepted traces whose final answers pass a verifier. For hard math problems, however, such traces can be rare under independent Monte Carlo (MC) sampling. To address this, we propose Diverse Alternative Reasoning Traces (DART), a trace-mining method that starts from a rejected trace, decomposes it into reasoning steps, and ranks them by position-weighted uncertainty. It then generates deliberately distinct alternative candidates for highly ranked steps using reference-answer guidance and a meta-thought before completing the resulting traces. On greedy-unsolved DeepMath-103K problems, DART recovers 37% more problems than MC sampling at a matched number of generated traces. Its estimated generation cost per recovered problem is nearly identical, while its cost per accepted trace is 30% lower. Post-training Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on traces mined by DART achieves the highest point estimate in five of six evaluations across MATH-500 and AIME benchmarks. These results demonstrate that revisiting rejected traces with DART can expand problem coverage and provide effective post-training data.

Some new methods.title: $μ$-Bench: Benchmarking Multi-User Task Completion in Shared Interaction Voice Agents
Some new methods.summary: Voice agents in shared spaces must satisfy interdependent multi-user requests while upholding per-user authority, privacy, and task constraints. Existing evaluations offer limited coverage when participants react throughout a session. We introduce $μ$-Bench, a benchmark for joint task completion in closed-loop, full-duplex multi-user voice interaction. Simulated participants act from isolated profiles of goals, knowledge, and permissions, adapting to the agent's speech and tool outcomes. Across 20 domains, 100 scenarios vary group size, acoustics, and follow-up demands to form 800 cases (408 tool-augmented, 392 tool-free). Joint Task Success (JTS) requires all user goals, privacy boundaries, and terminal states to hold jointly, while Pure JTS further disallows unauthorized tool calls; Attribution, Threading, and Coordination (ATC) diagnostics localize failures. Across 13 voice agents, proprietary systems peak at 62.24\% tool-free and 65.44\% tool-augmented success, while open-weight models remain below 20\%. ATC diagnostics show that open-weight models lag primarily in multi-turn attribution and threading, and controlled contrasts reveal that larger groups consistently degrade joint task success across capable systems. By coupling reactive multi-user simulation with verifiable session-level outcomes, $μ$-Bench provides a rigorous testbed for shared voice agents.

Some new methods.title: Enhancing Maritime Domain Awareness using Latent Space Representations
Some new methods.summary:
This work presents a novel application of Earth Observation (EO) embeddings for Maritime Domain Awareness (MDA) from the perspective of the geospatial foundation model TerraMind. By operating directly on compressed latent-space representations rather than on the original Sentinel-1 imagery, this approach directly addresses the data gravity bottleneck that increasingly constrains operational EO processing, in line with the objectives of the Embed2Scale project. In particular, linear and non-linear probing of compressed embeddings, latent space representations of synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imagery, is used to detect, localise, and characterise vessels from Sentinel-1 GRD images. Vessel detection achieves a ROC-AUC of 0.95, while vessel localisation has a median error of around 300 m for vessels longer than 100 m, and vessel AIS type-code classification achieves 62% accuracy for the majority classes. The latter, however, is highly correlated with vessel length. These results reveal both the potential and current limitations of Geospatial Foundation Models (GeoFMs) when applied to fine-grained MDA understanding in real-world scenarios.
  Additionally, a new maritime remote sensing dataset is released, pairing about 2,000 Sentinel-1 images with temporally aligned AIS signals from commercial vessels. Through manual inspection, each candidate sample was verified for bounding-box quality and for consistency between the AIS-reported vessel length and the observed vessel extent, cross-checking vessel identity and location against publicly available vessel records and, where available, photographs. The dataset was made ready for use with the NeuCo-Bench neural compression benchmark framework, publicly available on HuggingFace through https://huggingface.co/datasets/embed2scale/S1-single-ship-downstream .

Some new methods.title: AltRA-Test: An Alternative Annotator Test for LLM Judges Without Shared Annotators
Some new methods.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as judges and graders to replace human annotators, raising the question of when such replacement is statistically justified. To support such decisions, the Alternative Annotator Test (Alt-Test) was introduced for dense settings where all items are annotated by the same annotators. However, in many large-scale annotation settings, items are annotated by different subsets of annotators. We therefore propose the Alternative Annotator Test with Resampled Annotations (AltRA-Test), a statistical test that does not require that all items are annotated by the same annotators. AltRA-Test uses a bootstrap that resamples items, draws k human annotations for each item, and substitutes one of them with an LLM annotation. This produces paired all-human and mixed human-LLM panels. A replacement is supported when the inter-annotator agreement (IAA) of the mixed panel is statistically non-inferior to the IAA of the all-human panel, i.e., when the LLM preserves the signal that the human annotators share. We establish that AltRA-Test is a consistent test of asymptotic level alpha. We then evaluate it through simulations and real-world experiments in which we test 18 LLMs and 5 prompting techniques on 20 datasets across text, image, audio, and video. Across these evaluations, about 100 items often suffice for the test. In simulations, where we know whether the LLM is a better or a worse annotator than the humans, AltRA-Test makes more correct replacement decisions than existing baselines. In real-world data experiments, LLMs pass the test in about half of the setups, depending mainly on the task. Since replacement is not always justified, we encourage researchers to test it for their task.

Some new methods.title: Interpretable and Accurate Hybrid Decision Trees with Selective Case-Based Splits
Some new methods.summary: Decision trees are among the most well-known interpretable models in Machine Learning. Over the years, a wide variety of strategies have been proposed to define split conditions within the greedy learning framework, aiming to guide instance routing and enhance predictive performance. These strategies range from axis-parallel and oblique splits based on feature values to proximity-based splits using exemplar instances and more complex hybrid approaches. However, no single method has emerged as universally superior. In this work, we present two key contributions to the construction of greedy decision trees. First, we propose a hybrid tree architecture that integrates both feature-based and case-based splits, allowing for heterogeneous splits throughout the tree. Second, we introduce a novel type of split that leverages a selective case-based approach: when a split is needed, our method searches for the most informative subset of features to define the split, effectively balancing the specificity of case-based methods with the simplicity of feature-based ones. Experiments on a diverse set of tabular datasets show that our method outperforms standard decision trees and achieves performance on par with ensemble methods, while producing shallow trees that retain or even improve predictive accuracy.

Some new methods.title: How Much Do Coding Agents Over-Edit, and Why? An Empirical Study of Unneeded Edits in Repository-Level Agent Patches
Some new methods.summary: Agent patches are larger than developers', which is widely read as over-editing. But patch size does not say whether the extra edits are needed, what they are, or where they come from. We introduce Delta Residue Attribution (DRA), which replays agent trajectories, traces every block (unit) of the final patch to the step that wrote it, reverts each unit, and reruns the task tests to decide whether the unit is needed. We apply DRA to 7,660 resolved GitHub Copilot CLI trajectories from 18 frontier models on SWE-bench Verified (6,728) and DeepSWE (932), and grade developer patches using the same method. Agent patches do change more lines than developers'; on SWE-bench Verified the majority of extra edits add tests (61%) and documentation (13%) while on DeepSWE, most extra edits are code (58%). On both benchmarks, agents' code is on average at least as necessary as developers' (mean $NP_{code}$ 0.887 vs. 0.864 on SWE-bench Verified, where 11 of 18 models leave less unneeded code than developers, and 0.797 vs. 0.785 on DeepSWE). On average, 11% of an agent patch's code units on SWE-bench Verified are still unneeded, and 89% of those change behavior. Debug steps write almost none of the unneeded code. Code necessity differs substantially by model; it is unrelated to resolve rate on SWE-bench Verified and negatively correlated with it on DeepSWE (Spearman -0.59, p = 0.01). On SWE-bench Verified, pruning with DRA using only the tests the agent can see (its own tests and the repository's) removes the majority of unneeded code but also some needed code (67% recall, 46% precision), and 89% of pruned patches still resolve the task; asking the agent to audit its own diff is more precise but less effective (36% recall, 66% precision). We recommend that benchmarks report code necessity next to resolve rate and that over-editing be addressed through model training and harness-level pruning.

Some new methods.title: Shape-Aware Three-Way Merge for RDF Knowledge Graphs: The schema defines the conflict: an implementation and evaluation
Some new methods.summary: Merging RDF serializations creates ordering conflicts and misses semantic ones. We describe and evaluate a three-way merge in which the schema defines a conflict: set algebra combines canonical triples, and a slot is contended only where a SHACL shape bounds its cardinality and both sides' changes cannot stand within that bound. Unbounded predicates union; contended slots go to a person. The same shapes graph validates the result. We do not claim the first three-way merge for RDF. Our contribution is an implementation in a production multi-agent store and an evaluation against a reimplementation of Quit Store's Context Merge overlap rule, which it extends rather than replaces, and six other strategies. Across five synthetic seeds, the shape-aware operator raised 33 conflicts, all true positives as judged by the same shapes that define them, with no triples lost or fabricated and no SHACL violations admitted. The context-overlap baseline, counted per slot, detected the same 33 conflicts but asked 845 questions. A replay built from recorded production incidents covers 105 human alias repairs (93 after excluding 12 chained pairs) and 939 duplicate-value incidents. It reproduces a triple-level limit: different names for one entity remain invisible (0 of 93 alias repairs detected, matching 0 of 21 synthetic cases). In a study of evolving shape contracts, merging shape declarations first handles the tested cardinality changes, while datatype evolution exposes a detector blind spot caught by post-merge validation. An oracle that reads no shapes agrees with the shipped operator on the facts and history of all 23 reachable single-slot cases. Under wrong shapes, a missing bound loses data silently and a spurious one only adds questions. The supported claim is fewer human decisions with nothing silently lost, for cardinality conflicts in one deployment, not general merge correctness.
Some new methods.comment: 19 pages. Artifact, benchmark and replay corpus at https://github.com/intigraph/quipu ; every table names the command that regenerates it

Some new methods.title: A Survey of Security, Privacy, and Ethics of Large Language Models in Telecom
Some new methods.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into telecommunications for customer service, network analytics, and operational support. While offering efficiency and innovation, their deployment raises critical privacy, security, and ethical challenges due to the uniquely sensitive and longitudinal nature of telecom data. This paper presents a survey of LLM risks and safeguards in telecom context. Our survey introduces a telecom-specific taxonomy linking privacy, security, and ethics with use cases and outlines open research challenges such as longitudinal data privacy, cross-border compliance, and scalable guardrails.
Some new methods.comment: 5 pages, 1 figure, published in COMSNETS 2025 conference

Some new methods.title: RePace: Reasoning about Demonstration Speedup for Faster Vision-Language-Action Policies
Some new methods.summary: Since vision-language-action (VLA) policies can inherit the slow pace of human demonstrations, accelerating these demonstrations before fine-tuning can lead to faster VLA policies without an additional speed-selection module at deployment. Several offline speedup methods have focused on identifying segments that require less precision and assigning predefined speedup factors to the segments. However, even within a single segment, a speedup factor suitable for steady motion may be too high when precise alignment is required. To this end, this paper presents RePace, an offline reasoning framework that determines how much to accelerate each part of a demonstration. For the same recorded movement, RePace measures how much each candidate speedup factor shortens the sequence and compares the resulting observation-action pairs used for training. Given the task instruction, a pretrained language model uses the visual context and original motion of successive windows to interpret these candidate retiming effects and select a speedup profile for the complete episode. Experimental results demonstrate that RePace outperforms the baselines in overall task execution efficiency on both LIBERO and RoboCasa-Kitchen. On all three tasks with a gripper-equipped Franka Research 3 arm, RePace matches or exceeds the acceleration baselines in success rate and completes successful trials faster.

Some new methods.title: BOP-Refer: Benchmark for Monocular 3D and 2D Object Grounding
Some new methods.summary: We introduce BOP-Refer, the first benchmark for monocular 3D and 2D grounding of everyday and industrial objects sourced from 9 diverse BOP datasets. We pair images from these datasets with VLM-generated and human-verified referring expressions, and derive accurate ground-truth 3D and 2D bounding boxes of the referred objects from their 3D models and 6DoF pose annotations. Our systematic evaluation of 17 frontier VLMs across the major proprietary and open-weight families (Gemini, GPT, Claude, Qwen, Gemma) shows that the best model, Gemini 4 Carbon, reaches 72.6% AP_IoU2D in 2D but only 12.4% AP_IoU3D in 3D, despite the more lenient IoU thresholds in 3D. The predicted 3D boxes are usually centered on the target objects in the image but often off in depth by more than the object's size, suggesting that metric scale estimation, which needs reliable object size priors, is currently by far the main source of error.

Some new methods.title: From Prediction to Decision: Decision-Focused Fine-Tuning of Autoregressive Tabular Transformers for Cost-Sensitive Financial Events
Some new methods.summary: Autoregressive transformers trained on tokenized tabular event streams are a simple and strong baseline for predicting financial events such as fraud. Yet institutions do not act on probabilities; they act on decisions whose consequences are asymmetric and heteroscedastic: the cost of a missed high-value fraud and that of a wrongly declined small purchase are not the same. The standard bridge is post-hoc Bayes-optimal thresholding of calibrated probabilities under a cost matrix. We ask whether fine-tuning the model to the decision objective can do better. We fine-tune the same pretrained model so that its restricted softmax over label tokens (already a distribution over business actions) maximizes expected utility under an institution-specified, amount-scaled cost matrix. Because the reward is a known function of (action, outcome, amount) and the outcome is observed in the data, the expected-utility objective and its gradient are available in closed form. This is example-dependent cost-sensitive learning whose per-example loss is linear in the predicted probability, with no sampling, critics, or advantage estimation. A KL anchor to the pretrained model and an auxiliary language-modeling term preserve calibration and the generative event model. A sampled, group-normalized (GRPO-style) variant provides the extension point to trajectory-level rewards.

Some new methods.title: DRBench Pro: A Knowledge-Centric Benchmark for Professional Deep Research Agents
Some new methods.summary: Deep research agents gather information from multiple sources and synthesize it into reports on complex, open-ended questions. Existing benchmarks assess report quality along several dimensions, but lack a dedicated knowledge-centric evaluation of which research directions a report covers and how deeply it explores them. We introduce DRBench Pro, a benchmark that makes structured knowledge coverage the primary evaluation target. Our automated pipeline builds local knowledge trees from Wikipedia and uses sampled subgraphs to generate research queries and evidence-grounded rubrics. Each rubric corresponds to a relation in the tree, preserving the structure of the knowledge being evaluated. Agents receive only the research query. This structure allows us to measure breadth across major research directions and depth along related knowledge chains, with their geometric mean giving overall coverage. The benchmark includes 144 cases across 24 domains and 44,102 rubrics. Evaluating 16 deep research agents reveals different strengths in breadth and depth, with the best-performing agent reaching 57.04% overall coverage. Rubric judgments agree closely with human annotations, and agent rankings remain stable across the tested metric configurations.

Some new methods.title: Network of Theseus (like the ship)
Some new methods.summary: A standard assumption in deep learning is that the inductive bias introduced by a neural network architecture must persist from training through inference. The architecture you train with is the architecture you deploy. This assumption constrains the community from selecting architectures that may have desirable efficiency or design properties due to difficulties with optimization. We challenge this assumption with the Network of Theseus (NoT), a method for progressively converting a trained, or even untrained, guide network architecture part-by-part into an entirely different target network architecture while preserving the performance of the guide network. At each stage, components in the guide network architecture are incrementally replaced with the target architecture modules and aligned via representational similarity metrics. This procedure preserves most of the functionality of the guide network even under substantial architectural changes-for example, converting a convolutional network into a multilayer perceptron, or GPT-2 into a recurrent neural network. By decoupling optimization from deployment, NoT expands the space of viable inference-time architectures, opening opportunities for better accuracy-efficiency tradeoffs and enabling more directed exploration of the architectural design space.

Some new methods.title: Frozen Factor or Spectral Band? In LoRA, the Factor Matters More at Low Rank
Some new methods.summary: On two main task-model pairs, at ranks 1 to 8 with few optimiser steps, the factor a LoRA variant freezes matters more than its band of singular directions. MiCA and PiCa are compared by band, minor against dominant, yet MiCA freezes the output factor B and PiCa, in our notation, the input factor A. We cross factor and band in a 2 x 2 design on models from 1B to 8B parameters. Freezing A beats freezing B on both bands, by +12 to +20 points at rank 2 on a format task, our primary evidence, and still by about +7 points at rank 8 on OpenBookQA. A Holm correction over 258 primary tests, added post hoc, keeps this advantage in 15 of 16 tests and the lead of factor over band at ranks 1, 2 and 4, rank 1 of the format task being itself post hoc. At rank 8 that lead passes its own test but not the correction. The advantage repeats at rank 2 with two 7B models, by +11 to +13 points. Outside the correction, it repeats on GSM8K with a 1B model and, in a post hoc experiment, with an 8B model at ranks 8 and 16. It holds when B frozen gets as many parameters or more, with a random frozen A, and with sixteen times the format-task budget. It narrows above rank 8 on most pairs, at rank 8 with the 8B model on the two main tasks, on ARC and in a task mixture, and it closes at the last step of longer training on OpenBookQA. At MiCA's and PiCa's own settings, it is smaller or not detected.
Some new methods.comment: v2: rewritten; crossed factor-by-band design with pre-specified tests; eight seeds; ranks 1 to 64; 7B and 8B models; GSM8K. 42 pages

Some new methods.title: AI Lifecycle-Aware Feasibility Framework for Split-RIC Orchestration in NTN O-RAN
Some new methods.summary: Integrating Artificial Intelligence (AI) into Non-Terrestrial Networks (NTN) is constrained by the joint limits of satellite Size, Weight, and Power (SWaP), feeder-link capacity, and orbital connectivity, which directly affect O-RAN closed-loop control and AI lifecycle management. This paper studies the feasibility of distributing the O-RAN intelligence across Ground, LEO, and GEO segments through three representative deployments: (i) Ground-Centric control with telemetry streaming, (ii) a ground-LEO Split-RIC with on-board inference and store-and-forward model refresh, and (iii) GEO-LEO multi-layer control enabled by inter-satellite links. For each deployment, we derive closed-form expressions for lifecycle energy, near-real-time control latency, and model-refresh latency, while explicitly enforcing power-feasible spaceborne computational throughput. Pairwise analytical boundaries and numerical sensitivity analysis over telemetry volume, feeder-link conditions, inference workload, model longevity, and orbital waiting time identify the operating regions in which different placements are energetically preferable or satisfy model-refresh requirements. The results show that the architecture choice is inherently lifecycle- and constraint-dependent, providing decision-enabling primitives for Service Management and Orchestration (SMO) level AI placement and lifecycle orchestration in NTN O-RAN.
Some new methods.comment: 16 pages, 8 figures. Major revision following peer review: corrected power-feasible computation, energy and latency models, numerical results, and feasibility boundaries. Revised manuscript submitted to IEEE Transactions on Network and Service Management

Some new methods.title: Probing Visual Idiosyncrasies in Text-to-Image Models
Some new methods.summary: Text-to-Image (T2I) models turn short text descriptions into images, and the leading models now produce images of comparable visual quality. Whether their outputs still carry model-specific characteristics matters for attribution, for model comparison beyond aggregate quality, and for evaluations that assume anonymity. We ask whether images from frontier T2I models can still be classified by source, and which visual properties make this possible. Here we show that a standard ResNet-50 identifies the source of an image among HiDream-O1-Dev, FLUX.2-dev, HunyuanImage-3.0, and Qwen-Image-2512, the four highest-ranked open-source models on the Text-to-Image Arena, with 100.00% accuracy on held-out prompts. Human participants reach only 62.61% on the pairwise version of this task, so the distinguishing cues are not visually obvious. They are also not tied to a particular classifier and survive severe image corruptions and out-of-distribution prompts. We trace them to visual idiosyncrasies at three levels. Low-level texture statistics alone let a lightweight multi-layer perceptron match ResNet-50. Object layout, depth, and albedo estimated from the images each carry a source signal. Image captions reveal model-specific preferences in style and background that the prompts never specify. A one-sentence hint about these cues raises human accuracy by 9.03 percentage points. These idiosyncrasies make source classification a tool for measuring similarity between models and between real and generated images, and they caution against assuming anonymity in human preference evaluation of T2I models.

Some new methods.title: STAR-XPC: Set Transformer for Estimating X-ray Transmission in Polymer Composites
Some new methods.summary: Evaluating the energy transmission ratio of an X-ray beam through a polymer composite is a challenging task in radiation shielding studies. The reference solution with Monte Carlo transport simulation is highly accurate but computationally expensive: each of our reference simulations is capped at $4\times10^9$ photon histories and a 20,000 s (over 5 hours) time limit, while closed-form analytical methods fail to represent such complex scenarios. We present an artificial neural network model that maps the unordered multi-set of molecular constituents, their mass fractions, and four bulk physical descriptors directly to the transmission ratio $I(t)/I_0$ in 1-3 milliseconds. The model is a Set Transformer, which makes it permutation invariant by construction and accepts mixtures of different sizes up to 11 constituents within a fixed-size padded set. Each constituent is embedded with a chemistry-pretrained transformer language model, ChemBERTa. In our proposed method, training data are produced by an automated PENELOPE/penEasy pipeline using the radiation source at 30, 80, 100, and 120 kV tube voltages over polyethylene-based shielding composite slabs of thicknesses spanning 0.15-2.5 mm. After preprocessing, the dataset contains $n = 4697$ simulated configurations on which a leakage-free, jointly stratified 10-fold cross-validation is performed, attaining mean squared error MSE = $(1.12 \pm 0.56)\times10^{-4}$, normalized-MSE percentage NMSE% = 0.0294% $\pm$ 0.0147%, and $R^2 = 0.9988$. The corresponding per-sample percentage errors give an alpha-trimmed ($α= 0.10$) absolute percentage error (APE) of 1.66% and a median APE of 1.15%. Our model's inference is several orders of magnitude faster than the underlying Monte Carlo simulation (sub-millisecond per query vs. several hours for the reference run) with effective accuracy in predicting $I(t)/I_0$.

Some new methods.title: Knowledge-Base Gradient Descent: Self-Structuring Learning through Question Answering
Some new methods.summary: We consider the problem of constructing knowledge bases for applications based on large language models, in which the structure of a knowledge base determines how an application can retrieve and connect the information needed to answer a question. We study Self-Structuring Learning, a setting in which questions and expected answers guide the construction of a persistent knowledge base whose editable structure can be a graph schema or the organization of linked knowledge documents. We propose Knowledge-Base Gradient Descent, which diagnoses discrepancies between expected answers and responses obtained through the current knowledge base. At each round, the method proposes a structural edit, rebuilds the knowledge base, and adopts the edit when the learning loss decreases. The retained structure is evaluated on other questions about the same sources. By randomizing over candidate edits, we express the loss change of an edit as a derivative with respect to the probability of selecting it, and we evaluate joint edits as single candidates because their changes interact. Schema Descent instantiates the method for graph schemas. In experiments on large documents, each a bundle of research papers, the updated knowledge cards and graph schemas obtain higher mean Answer F1 on held-out generated questions than their initial structures, with schema gains in every document. On human questions, mean F1 rises for schemas and falls for cards: the updated structures serve the kind of question they were learned from.

Some new methods.title: Repairing the Trustworthiness of Distilled Language Models
Some new methods.summary: Knowledge distillation enables the deployment of large language models through smaller student models, but the compression process can introduce regressions in trustworthiness even when downstream performance is preserved. Repairing such failures is challenging because the original distillation corpus is often unavailable, while direct preference optimization may alter capabilities inherited from the teacher. We propose a targeted repair framework based on the proximal Bregman response function (PBRF) that addresses both limitations. We estimate the curvature required for PBRF using a surrogate proxy dataset, removing dependence on the original transfer corpus, and extend the framework to preference-based supervision through an odds-ratio objective. This enables the use of preferred and dispreferred response pairs while constraining changes to the distilled model. Our results show that the proposed approach improves targeted trustworthiness behaviors for both pre-training and post-training models while largely preserving downstream performance, providing a practical alternative to re-distillation or unconstrained preference optimization. Our experiment results show that across different distilled models, the trustworthy regression can be improved by up to 8% with less than 1% decrement in perplexity.

Some new methods.title: Not all world models can doubt: how training objective and architecture shape epistemic uncertainty in JEPA and RSSM world models
Some new methods.summary: World models predict how an environment responds to actions, so that candidate actions can be evaluated before execution. Executed actions, or decisions, taken in this manner are only as reliable as the model's predictive capabilities, and predictions in turn are only reliable within the model's experience. Epistemic uncertainty (EU) is the signal that marks where that experience ends. In this work we offer an extensive empirical study on how training objectives and architectures shape epistemic uncertainty of world models. More precisely, we present a controlled comparison of post-hoc EU (last-layer Laplace and ensembles) between two dominant models of different paradigms: 1) LeWorldModel (LeWM): A joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA), which predicts the next embedding without a decoder, and 2) DreamerV3: A recurrent state-space model (RSSM), which reconstructs the observation from a recurrent latent state. In ten simulated visual-control environments, we follow a controlled state perturbation of the environment state through every stage of the models up to the final EU estimate. We find that the RSSM attenuates the state perturbation through two mechanisms before it reaches an estimator on the predictor feature. Its recurrent update averages over context, so a change in a single frame reaches the state at a fraction of its size and recovers only as the change persists. Its reconstruction objective weights an entity by the pixels it covers, so a small object can be lost due to the training objective. The JEPA has neither mechanism and passes the change through all stages to the uncertainty. We further show that this translates to gaps in five uncertainty related downstream tasks, from unfamiliar-state detection to uncertainty-penalised planning: the RSSM uncertainty misses deviations that its own posterior registers, whereas the JEPA uncertainty reports what its model sees.

Some new methods.title: Transferring Architecture as an Optimization Prior
Some new methods.summary: Initialization determines the optimization "fate" of a model, going far beyond just setting the scale of its weights. It establishes a fundamental initial geometry over the input data, dictating certain aspects such as which examples are considered close and which representations gradient descent will naturally refine first. In this paper, we view the initial geometry of a network as an optimization prior and ask whether a network can change its optimization prior by referencing a completely different architecture. To investigate this question, we use an initialization procedure where a target network is aligned to the representational geometry of a randomly initialized guide network before any downstream training occurs. Crucially, alignment to the guide network cannot transfer learned features, never receives gradients, and does not use labels. We demonstrate that this cross-architecture transfer of "fate" benefits the target network in two key domains: (1) instilling the optimization benefits of depth into shallow networks by aligning them to deeper networks, and (2) transferring representational granularity by using fine-resolution networks to shape the geometry of networks with coarser representations. In both cases, the alignment results in improved downstream performance of the target network. Ultimately, this demonstrates that a model's architectural destiny can be decoupled from its physical structure and explicitly modified at initialization.

Some new methods.title: Solve Vision with Code: Coding Agents Are Stronger Visual Reasoners Than Video Models
Some new methods.summary: Video generation models are increasingly evaluated as visual reasoners: given a first frame and a natural-language prompt, can the model produce the video in which the specified task is carried out? The paradigm is considered advantageous because the reasoning is native to the visual medium, unfolding directly in the frames rather than through language or code. Whether this native route is in fact the more reliable path to visual reasoning has not been tested against a symbolic alternative under the same conditions. We therefore pose the same tasks, with identical inputs, output specification and evaluator, to both media: rather than denoising pixels, a coding agent writes a program that renders the answer video, which an unmodified rule-based evaluator scores. On VBVR-Pro-Bench (Xu et al., 2026), a 500-instance suite spanning five cognitive categories with symbolic ground truth, the agent receives the same first frame and prompt as the video model, with no access to ground truth, metadata or generation models, and one attempt per instance. Three closed-model agents (Codex with gpt-6-astra, Claude Code with Fable 5.1 and Gemini CLI with Gemini 3.1 Pro) score 0.923, 0.894 and 0.893, each more than 0.22 above the strongest video model. Among 23 runnable open-weight models, the best, GLM-5, reaches 0.572, above all video models except the RL-trained one. Together, we show that for tasks whose solutions can be computed from a first frame and a prompt, program synthesis is currently a substantially more reliable route to visual reasoning than video generation.
