A fully GPU-based ingest pipeline applies insert/delete/modify batches at up to 29 million edges per second, 4.5 times faster than the host path. An exact dynamic-programming oracle selects zero folds on every tested workload under its action space and calibrated cost model. Standard folding heuristics use 4 to 15 times more GPU time and up to 4 times more persistent device storage. End to end, RecTile improves the time-storage tradeoff on all five evolving-graph workloads, including delete-heavy streams. It is also fastest on a dense stress stream with 1220 records per tile. There, folding uses 1.3 times less peak persistent storage but takes 3.9 times more time. For the evolving graph-like, interleaved update/SpMV workloads evaluated here, the mutable record store can serve directly as the compute representation.
Container scheduling.comment: 8 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables. Presented at BAŞARIM 2026, the 9th National High Performance Computing Conference, İstanbul, Türkiye, October 14-16, 2026. Code: https://github.com/tweetpie/RecTile

Container scheduling.title: MotionServe: Efficient Multi-Robot Serving by Exploiting Robot Execution Slack
Container scheduling.summary: As robotic arms undertake diverse manipulation tasks, a deployment may need to serve many task-specific vision-language-action (VLA) policies concurrently. Dedicating a GPU to each robot is costly, motivating shared-GPU inference. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) allows compatible policies to share a frozen backbone with lightweight policy-specific adapters, reducing model-weight memory and enabling cross-policy batching. However, robot inference must keep pace with physical execution. With action chunking, robots continue executing buffered actions while awaiting new predictions, and the remaining buffered time provides each robot's execution slack for serving its next request. Once this slack is exhausted, the robot stalls until new actions arrive, interrupting task progress. Observing earlier preserves more slack but can lead to disruptive replanning and lower task success, whereas delaying dispatch to form larger batches can improve GPU efficiency but consumes slack and risks stalls. To balance these competing demands, we present MotionServe, a shared-GPU serving system that coordinates robot observation timing with server-side batch formation. MotionExec selects observation triggers based on motion structure in predicted action chunks, allowing inference to overlap with remaining buffered execution. SlackBatch combines the resulting per-robot execution budgets with estimated outstanding GPU work to determine when to wait, which requests to batch, and when to dispatch them. We evaluate X-VLA on LIBERO and SimplerEnv's WidowX tasks and OpenVLA-OFT on LIBERO, with up to 96 simulated robots sharing one NVIDIA H200 GPU. At 96 robots, MotionServe reduces mean stall per episode by 43.4% and 32.6% and improves task success by 8.98 and 2.30 percentage points, respectively, over each model's lowest-stall baseline. Backbone sharing also reduces weight memory for 96 policies by 97.6% and 91.1%.

Container scheduling.title: Cascade: Exploiting SLO-Aware latency budget for fair and high goodput LLM inference serving
Container scheduling.summary:
The reasoning and agentic capabilities of LLMs have expanded the range of applications they support, from short interactive exchanges to long, prefix-heavy requests. LLM serving platforms today define response-latency service-level objectives (SLOs), yet requests under the same SLO differ by orders of magnitude in input length, generation length, execution cost, and reusable KV-cache availability, leaving each request with a different amount of latency headroom. This headroom must cover not only execution, but also scheduling and preemption delays and the cost of retrieving KV state from deeper memory tiers. Existing systems manage these decisions independently, despite their combined impact on latency.
  We present Cascade, an LLM serving system that coordinates these decisions using a per-request latency budget: the difference between a request's SLO and its predicted remaining service time, continuously updated from request characteristics, KV-cache state, and system load. Cascade uses this budget to prioritize requests and to decide how much non-resident KV state to prefetch from deeper tiers, with the remainder fetched on demand or recomputed given the serving system. On production traces across three LLMs, Cascade improves goodput by 10.4x over vLLM and 1.8x over a SLO-aware scheduler, and reduces SLO violations by 76% and 31%, respectively, while remaining fair across heterogeneous requests.

Container scheduling.title: Fast 4-bit KV-Cache Decoding on Hopper GPUs: Why Existing Kernels Are Slow and How to Fix Them
Container scheduling.summary: A 4-bit KV cache reads about half the bytes of FP8, but Hopper GPUs have no FP4 hardware and little instruction-issue capacity per byte of memory bandwidth, so 4-bit values must be decoded in software. On H200, vLLM's NVFP4 KV path (FlashInfer's decode) reaches 10-20% of memory bandwidth and is up to 1.7x slower than FP8. NVBit instruction counts show two causes: the kernels behind vLLM's 4-bit paths (FlashInfer NVFP4, Triton UltraQuant) execute 2-6x Hopper's issue budget per byte and serialize loading, decoding and matrix multiplies. Our Hopper-native decode kernel overlaps a TMA producer warp with two compute warpgroups, lays the cache out at write time so decoded values feed the tensor cores from registers, and swaps the matrix operands so small query groups need no padding. On H200 it reaches 67-75% of peak bandwidth at batch 32-128 and at all 11 shapes is 1.12-1.49x faster than the faster of XQA and FlashAttention-4's proposed native FP8. Inside vLLM, with an accuracy recipe (K mean removal and rotation, 4 BF16 sink tokens, BF16 layer 0), it decodes 1.12-1.64x faster per step on Llama-3.1-8B than vLLM's FlashInfer FP8 path at batch 8 and above (1.04-1.24x over FlashAttention-4's FP8), is level at batch 1, and holds 1.63x as many tokens. On one H200 under a reasoning-like request stream, the highest rate at which 99% of requests meet the latency targets is 1.23-1.32x FP8's on Llama-3.1-8B and 1.67-2.20x on Qwen2.5-72B, as the cache becomes the limit; prefill-heavy streams are worse (7% slower prefill). On five 7B-32B models, repeated runs show no significant accuracy difference from BF16 KV. In Qwen2-family models, whose reasoning variants collapse under FP8 KV, layer 0's key mean is almost entirely the key-projection bias identified by prior work, seen through RoPE and computable from the weights alone; keeping that layer in BF16 restores FP8 KV and, with K mean removal, 4-bit KV.

Container scheduling.title: Purlin: Separating Orchestration from the Datapath of Collectives
Container scheduling.summary: Distributed inference depends on GPU collective communication that must keep pace with evolving hardware and specialized workloads. However, existing works often couple the semantics, orchestration (where and when data moves), and datapath (how data moves) of collective communication. This coupling makes it costly to adopt new hardware mechanisms and customize communication for applications. We present Purlin, a scale-up communication framework that separates these concerns. At the top of Purlin, we specify collectives as a transformation from an input to an output layout. In the middle, we introduce a shared protocol, Stage, Notify, And Consume (SNAC), which derives orchestration from these specifications. Below SNAC sits a hardware-specific datapath we call Atom, which implements two key data movement primitives for collectives: copy and reduce. This separation lets us customize collectives and adopt new hardware mechanisms while reusing orchestration via SNAC. We evaluate Purlin on A100, H200, and B200 GPUs. Across seven collectives, Purlin achieves latency speedups of up to 5.14x and bandwidth improvements of up to 4.50x over baselines. Integrated into SGLang, Purlin improves offline LLM serving throughput and interactivity by 1.13x on average and up to 1.37x over baselines. For online LLM inference, Purlin improves interactivity by 1.26x on average and up to 2.85x, with the largest gain occurring under overload. For diffusion image generation, Purlin reduces end-to-end latency by up to 1.13x.

Container scheduling.title: Sei Giga
Container scheduling.summary: We introduce the Sei Giga, a multi-concurrent producer parallelized execution EVM layer one blockchain. In an internal testnet Giga has achieved >5 gigagas/sec throughput and sub 250ms finality. Giga uses Autobahn for consensus with separate DA and consensus layers requiring f+1 votes for a PoA on the DA layer before consensus. Giga reaches consensus over ordering and uses async block execution and state agreement to remove execution from the consensus bottleneck.

Container scheduling.title: Measuring GPU Memory Traffic on the NVIDIA GB10 Without C2C Telemetry
Container scheduling.summary: The NVIDIA GB10, used in the DGX Spark and in desktop AI systems from several vendors, joins an Arm CPU die and a Blackwell GPU die with NVLink C2C. The GPU has no local memory, so every GPU access that misses in its L2 cache crosses C2C to the LPDDR5X attached to the CPU die. Yet the software on the systems we tested exposes no counter for this traffic. We show that five L2 sector counters of the GPU, sampled every 10 ms through NVIDIA's CUPTI sampling interface by a process that does not attach to the workload, measure GPU memory traffic live and separate copy engine traffic from the read misses and writes of GPU kernels. For large streaming transfers of known size, the counters agree within 0.28% on an Acer GN100 and within 0.005% on a DGX Spark, track the volume moved regardless of how it is split into copies, and exclude data reused in L2. The GPU's SMMU counter, a natural alternative, counts address translations rather than bytes. Applied to an unmodified server, the method shows Mistral 7B decode reading 13.47 GiB per token, the weights it uses plus its key value (KV) cache, at 83% of the memory bandwidth NVIDIA specifies. We release the method as an open source tool.

Container scheduling.title: The Complexity of Full-Information Iterated Protocols
Container scheduling.summary:
Full-information protocols are a common abstraction in distributed computing. In its iterated form, processes proceed through successive communication rounds in which each process shares its entire current knowledge of the execution. Usually, it is implicitly assumed that a process can transmit an unbounded amount of information in every round. This paper makes that assumption explicit and studies its computational cost.
  We formalize the problem of simulating iterated full-information protocols when communication is bounded, so that each process may share at most $b$ bits with every other process per round. We show that for a large family of shared-memory communication models and $n+1$ processes, simulating $r$ iterations of the full-information protocol requires \(Ω\!\left((n!)^{r-1} 2^{\,n-b}\right)\) rounds. We complement this lower bound with simulation algorithms that are asymptotically optimal in the conventional read-write model. In particular, the case of two processes is special: $r$ iterations of a full-information protocol can be simulated in exactly $r$ rounds while using only $2$-bit variables, as the amount of information that must be represented remains bounded for two processes but grows with each iteration for $n \geq 2$.
Container scheduling.comment: Journal version published in Theoretical Computer Science

Container scheduling.title: Packed-Ring Queues: Lock-Free and Wait-Free Concurrent Queues on GPU
Container scheduling.summary: Concurrent queues are a foundational building block of parallel programming. On CPUs, decades of research have produced queue designs with well-understood correctness and progress guarantees -- from lock-free rings to wait-free constructions. On GPUs, where queues increasingly sit on the critical path of device-side task graphs and GPU-initiated I/O, no comparable foundation exists: SIMT execution serializes divergent retries across a warp; tens of thousands of threads contend on the same counter words; the double-width atomics that several CPU designs assume are absent; and GPU memory models are weakly ordered, so the classical algorithms do not transfer unchanged. We present the packed-ring queues (PRQs) -- two linearizable, bounded GPU queues that represent each compound atomic state in one native word of at most 64 bits: (1) PRQ-LF, a lock-free ring whose warp-batched fast path issues one atomic per warp on each of the queue's contended words, and (2) PRQ-WF, a wait-free ring in which peer threads cooperatively complete any operation that falls behind. To the best of our knowledge, PRQ-WF is the first GPU concurrent queue whose wait-freedom is proved as a theorem, with no assumption about how the GPU schedules threads. Across four GPUs from two vendors (NVIDIA A100 and GH200, AMD MI210 and MI300A), PRQ-LF outperforms the blocking Broker Queue by 5.0-20.4x at 32K threads, and PRQ-WF sustains throughput under producer/consumer imbalance where a prior design completes fewer than 0.1% of its attempts.

Container scheduling.title: Two Rounds Are Already Hard for Loop-Free Updates of Routing Trees
Container scheduling.summary: Updating a routing tree can create loops even when the old and new trees lead to the same destination. A controller chooses which routers update in each round, but their updates may finish in any order. Strong loop freedom therefore requires every partial completion to be acyclic. We show that deciding whether two rounds suffice is NP-complete, even when a safe three-round schedule is supplied. The proof is a linear-size reduction from 3-SAT with one old clause spine and four routers per variable. Three types of mixed cycles enforce consistent literal choices and clause satisfaction. For every nonempty input formula, the constructed instance needs exactly two rounds if the formula is satisfiable and exactly three otherwise.

Container scheduling.title: Certified Split Windows for Parallel Lexing: Recovering Boundaries Where No Byte Certifies
Container scheduling.summary: A certified split point lets a parallel lexer cut unlexed input at one byte with the serial token stream provably preserved, but several conventional token sets in the predecessor's study certify no byte once string, comment, or whitespace-run forms are included (arXiv:2608.03473v2). We generalize from a byte to a bounded window, a byte string such that, whatever the context, the token covering its final byte begins at a known origin. Since the certificate is conditional on occurrence and may be vacuous, every applicability figure counts only windows carrying an asserted completely tokenizable occurrence witness. We give a conservative model of a maximal-munch scanner's possible histories across a window, prove it sound, and decide reachability in it exactly by exhausting a finite quotient of its reachable configurations. Within the flat, completely tokenizable scope, model-positive answers are semantic certificates; negatives are relative to the model, which refuses some windows a greedy scanner would allow. For both model and semantic certificates, existence is PSPACE-complete with or without a witness requirement, and a shortest window has $2^{Θ(n)}$ bytes in the worst case over at most $n$ live states. Two smaller searches decide plain model existence, the second shipped in release 2.2.0 of munch. Of 400 random token sets, 322 of the 337 certifying no byte gain witnessed windows and four more gain model certificates with occurrence unresolved. No model search reaches its threshold. The predecessor's exact-empty rows all gain witnessed windows of two to four bytes. A boundary profile marks each gap of an occurring window forced, crossed or open, and a window-local cut is sound exactly at forced gaps. Whether a given gap is ever a boundary and whether it is open are PSPACE-complete, while occurrence, the forced verdict and a given origin's certificate are NL-complete.
Container scheduling.comment: 53 pages, 4 tables. v4: existence of a certified window, for the model or the definition, with or without a witness, is PSPACE-complete and a shortest one has $2^{Θ(n)}$ bytes in the worst case; whether a gap is ever a boundary is PSPACE-complete, and a given origin's certificate NL-complete. Artifact: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21842344 . Companion to arXiv:2608.03473

Container scheduling.title: Certified Split Points for Parallel Lexing: Exact and Modulo Discarded Tokens
Container scheduling.summary: Table-driven DFA lexing is sequential, since each transition depends on the previous byte's state. Scanning one input in parallel needs each chunk's entry state, which existing methods recover by simulation, speculation, prescanning, or overlap. We give two conditions under which none is needed. For a longest-match scanner restarting from q0 at every token boundary, a byte b is a certified split symbol when no reachable state other than q0 has a b-transition whose target can reach acceptance, and q0 is not re-entrant if it has one. Every occurrence of such a byte in completely tokenizable input begins a token, so chunks starting there reproduce the serial sequence of kinds and lengths. The condition is necessary and sufficient, but one string, comment, or whitespace run can remove every useful certificate. Comments and whitespace are usually discarded, so we weaken the guarantee to equality after deleting a declared discarded set and give a second condition, a precomputed constant-time one-bit test. It is sound but incomplete and more permissive, strictly so on suitable token and discarded sets. It recovers newline for a conventional C-like tokenization and tab, newline and carriage return for JSON, and refuses newline where block comments are unrestricted. Safety modulo the discarded set is PSPACE-complete for general token automata and decidable in polynomial time for literal vocabularies, and every unsafe byte has a replayable counterexample. On the fifteen token sets studied the second condition is already exact. Splitting at exact certificates in munch reaches 92.6-95.3% parallel efficiency at eight threads on a restricted CPU set and a 512 MiB corpus, and a 3.46-3.94x end-to-end speedup at four threads, on one machine. It turns delimiter-based parallel lexing from a language-specific assumption into a property a compiler checks.
Container scheduling.comment: 52 pages, 2 figures, 4 tables. v5: proves safety modulo discarded tokens PSPACE-complete, already over three symbols, and that automata for the completely tokenizable inputs can need exponentially many states. Artifact: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24220471 . Certificate tables, composition figures and the validation sweep are generated from the compiled automata and asserted in CI

Container scheduling.title: Motivo: A Motif-Based Algorithm-Architecture Co-Design for Fast and Energy-Efficient Graph-Based Genome Analysis
Container scheduling.summary: Read mapping, a key step of genome sequence analysis, matches each fragment of a sequenced genome (a read) to its location in a reference genome. A genome graph is a graph-based reference genome that represents the genetic diversity of a population as alternative paths, and thus improves read mapping accuracy. However, the size and complexity of a genome graph make sequence-to-graph (S2G) mapping a major bottleneck. Prior software and hardware approaches for S2G mapping perform redundant costly operations (e.g., graph traversals and dynamic programming) that do not lead to valid mappings. Our key observation is that a genome graph consists of small subgraphs that share a limited set of recurring topologies, which we call motifs. We propose Motivo, a topology-aware algorithm-architecture co-design for S2G mapping. Motivo's algorithm uses motifs in two ways. First, it stores the precomputed motifs of each node in a compact index, which replaces a graph traversal with a single memory lookup. Second, it uses the topology of a motif and the properties of its nodes to identify the few most suitable mapping paths with arithmetic operations. The algorithm enables high-performance execution on CPUs and GPUs and high-performance, low-energy execution on Motivo-ASIC, an accelerator we co-design with it. Motivo-CPU provides 2.1-18.4x, 2.8-343x, and 1.4-10.1x speedups over GraphAligner, vg, and minigraph, and Motivo-GPU provides 1.5-1.6x speedups over vg-giraffe. Motivo-ASIC provides 7.4-11.7x (138-274x) speedups over state-of-the-art CPU-based tools for short (long) reads. Compared to SeGraM (short reads) and HARP (long reads), Motivo-ASIC achieves 5.3x and 4.0-4.3x higher throughput per Watt and 1.7x and 2.7-3.0x higher throughput per mm$^2$, respectively. Motivo maintains equal or higher mapping accuracy than other tools (96.8%-99.7%) for short and long reads on two types of genome graphs.

Container scheduling.title: CXL Coherence Writes Back What Surviving Hosts See, Leaving Flushes Only for Ordering
Container scheduling.summary: Hosts that share memory over Compute Express Link (CXL) cache its lines, and a host that crashes loses the lines it has modified and not written back. Designs for such memory stop every host when one crashes, assume stored energy, or flush after each operation. We show that when a crashing host's clients die with it, the flushes a host crash requires are those that keep one line from reaching the memory device before a line it depends on, and not those that make a finished operation durable. The reason is a property that CXL requires of the fabric: a modified line is written back before another host accesses it. Whatever a surviving host has seen is then on the device, and our crash condition lets a crash drop operations that only the crashed host observed. We prove the claim for operations that take effect in a single store, and test it on small instances of models of three published designs, whose operations store several times. A lock table needs no flush to keep the locks of surviving hosts. A persistent hash index keeps every operation a survivor has observed, and in two workloads it writes fewer than half as many lines to the device as its published code does. An allocator's flush of each new reference is neither sufficient nor necessary for the survivors' safety: the allocator lacks ordering flushes, one of them when a reference changes hands.

Container scheduling.title: LiZoneDedup: An End-to-End In-Storage Deduplication Architecture for ZNS SSDs
Container scheduling.summary: Data deduplication reduces write traffic and extends flash lifetime, especially on versioned workloads: container images, VM snapshots, and backups. Yet in-storage deduplication has never been implemented for emerging Zoned Namespace (ZNS) SSDs. Conventional designs require a page-level FTL to remap duplicate writes and a device-wide fingerprint index far exceeding controller DRAM; neither exists under ZNS. Our insight is that ZNS's append-only contract is a natural substrate for deduplication: a duplicate mapping, once recorded, is never modified in place, so dedup metadata becomes an append-only log rather than a mutable page-level table, and fingerprints fit in compact per-zone indexes rather than a global index. We present \sysname, the first complete in-storage deduplication architecture for ZNS, built around three mechanisms: a device-selected write primitive that hides zone placement from the host, content-based routing that confines each lookup to a small fixed set of candidate zones, and lifecycle-separated metadata with per-zone identity indexes and append-only reference counts. On a 1\,TB ZNS SSD, \sysname replaces the $\sim$10.7 GB global fingerprint index with per-zone indexes of a few hundred KB that become NAND-resident once sealed, holds controller DRAM at 37-50 MB (including a bounded-size metadata LRU cache) regardless of device capacity, improves logical write throughput by 1.1-3.5$\times$, cuts physical writes by up to 85\%, and reaches 91-99\% of the throughput of an infeasible page-FTL oracle.

Container scheduling.title: NoeVera: Can Knowledge Guide Experiments and Experiments Refine Knowledge?
Container scheduling.summary: With the growing demand for large language model (LLM) services, optimizing LLM serving systems is becoming increasingly complex, and the bottleneck is no longer predicting how a given configuration will perform. The harder problem is deciding what to investigate: which mechanisms matter for a workload, which configurations are worth testing, and what evidence a decision still needs. In this work, we present NoeVera, an agentic Second Brain that goes beyond just one-shot retrieval by turning papers, code, benchmarks, and experimental results into a persistent, provenance-preserving knowledge base with three planes: source evidence, reusable synthesis, and agent memory. Decision-aware retrieval assembles compact evidence packs, role-specific agents reason over them and invoke a simulator (Vidur or GAUSS) whenever quantitative support is needed, and every finding is written back as a scoped evidence record, so knowledge guides experiments and experiments refine knowledge. In configuration search over four serving scenarios, NoeVera comes within 5% of the optimum in a median of 6-7 simulator calls, versus 9 for Bayesian optimization and 15 for a knowledge-free agent with the same tools; on A100 GPUs, its representative configurations deliver ~1.30x vLLM-default throughput and meet every scenario's latency objective. When reused, provenance-preserving evidence records over-generalize on only 8% of applicability traps, versus 28% for a general-purpose agent memory. On the held-out 48-task split of a 72-task benchmark, NoeVera scores 29% higher than an equally equipped agent and 36% higher than its single-call retrieval counterpart (0.80 vs. 0.62 and 0.59), and even when baselines receive NoeVera's own prompts, a statistically significant part of its evidence-evolution advantage remains.

Container scheduling.title: Zarc: Exact Nearest Neighbors over a Billion Vectors in Seconds
Container scheduling.summary: Exact k-nearest-neighbor vector search lies on the critical path of machine learning systems, from sparse attention in the latest large language models (LLMs) to long-context memories and training-data deduplication. Exhaustive GPU search scans the whole dataset for every query, while approximate indexes return inexact neighbors. Recent methods skip almost every vector with a cheap half-precision proof that it lies too far away, but only on one GPU that holds the whole dataset. Our insight is to keep only the short rows of these proofs in GPU memory and to fetch the few remaining full vectors from host memory. Our system, Zarc, answers Euclidean, cosine, inner-product, and filtered queries exactly under updates. On four H100 GPUs, it answers 10,000 exact queries over one billion vectors in 1.1 seconds instead of five minutes. On eleven open LLMs, it retrieves the exact top-10 attention keys 2.2x to 13.1x faster than exhaustive search. In sparse attention over one million tokens, it runs 3.1x faster than bf16 selection with FlashInfer, which misses the exact top-64 for most queries.

Container scheduling.title: Residual-Weighted Randomized Jacobi: Sharpened Bounds via Residual Concentration and Asynchronous Extension
Container scheduling.summary:
We study randomized stationary methods for symmetric positive definite linear systems in which component $j$ is selected with probability proportional to $|r_j|^\ell$. This family interpolates between uniform sampling on the nonzero residual components ($\ell \to 0^+$) and Gauss--Southwell relaxation ($\ell \to \infty$). For $\ell = 2$ we sharpen the one-step analysis using the inverse participation ratio (IPR) of the residual, $ν^2(r) = n\|r\|_4^4/\|r\|_2^4$, which is $1$ for a uniform residual and approaches $n$ as it concentrates. The resulting bound multiplies the guaranteed expected-progress coefficient of uniform sampling by the IPR (and the expected progress, for constant-diagonal $A$).
  We extend the analysis to asynchronous execution via the Avron--Druinsky--Gupta (ADG) framework, obtaining, under an a priori envelope on the IPR, an epoch-based reduction bound in which the IPR controls both the progress coefficient and the certified delay window. Synchronous runs on three structured problems and eight Matrix Market matrices support the sharpened bound, and shared-memory experiments show an IPR trajectory nearly insensitive to concurrency. There, committing a buffered residual value (consistent reads, the easier case for ADG) led to divergence at high concurrency on every problem, while re-reading the component at update time (inconsistent reads) diverged in a minority of runs on one problem. We conjecture a feedback-damping mechanism, test its predictions, and find that sufficiently small fixed steps and an adaptive IPR-driven step-size rule removed the instability in every run, at a cost in speed.

Container scheduling.title: Ossim: OS-Driven Live Simulation for Cluster-Scale Full-Stack Evaluation (Extended Version)
Container scheduling.summary: Cluster-scale full-stack simulation is essential for evaluating distributed software stacks and emerging hardware components before deployment. Such simulation must achieve both full-stack fidelity for the unmodified production stack and the simulation performance required for iterative configuration exploration. However, no existing method achieves both. We present Ossim, an OS-level approach to cluster-scale full-stack simulation built on top of the Linux virtualization stack. Ossim comprises four subsystems: simulation-oriented scheduling, live memory hierarchy management, simulation-aware IPC, and multi-host coordination. Together, they coordinate live and modeled components under shared simulated time while controlling interference among co-located live VMs. These mechanisms point toward simulation-native OS support, where simulation control and orchestration become core OS responsibilities.
Container scheduling.comment: Extended version of the APSys'26 paper (arXiv:2606.18958). 14 pages, 7 figures, 3 tables

Container scheduling.title: ARC: Adaptive Rollout Control for Efficient Synchronous LLM Reinforcement Learning
Container scheduling.summary: Synchronous reinforcement learning (RL) for large language models proceeds through a repeated rollout--barrier--update loop. Each update must wait for a fixed number of complete, group-relative training samples, yet individual response lengths and reward outcomes vary widely and only emerge as generation progresses. Static admission and unconditional completion therefore leave accelerators idle in some steps, and waste computation generating samples that will never contribute to the current update. We present ARC, a closed-loop rollout architecture that governs synchronous RL rollout at group granularity. ARC uses \textit{Calibrated Streaming Backfill} to judge from partial observations whether a group is still worth completing, backfilling a fresh candidate immediately when it is not; \textit{Deferred Group Completion} to park an uncertain early stop and resume it later instead of discarding it outright, bounded by a resume-cycle limit that guarantees termination; and \textit{Adaptive Admission} and \textit{Pipelining} to order admitted samples by early-measured duration and to admit further candidates only while expected supply still falls short of the target number of accepted groups. Under online evaluation, ARC reduces rollout time by $37.4\%$, a $1.60\times$ speedup, and improves effective GRPO throughput by $50.1\%$ over existing baselines, while directly recovering 98.9\% of the training groups that would ultimately have been kept.

Container scheduling.title: When Does Decomposition Help? Empirical Study on Workload-Architecture Affinity in LLM Inference Serving
Container scheduling.summary: Large language model (LLM) inference can be organized as independent monolithic replicas, tensor- or pipeline-parallel serving groups, or disaggregated prefill and decode services. Although decomposition is often presented as a route to higher efficiency, its benefit depends on workload shape, model fit, and whether phase-specific resources can be independently scaled. Existing comparisons frequently change several of these factors at once. We isolate the architectural effect by evaluating five SGLang serving organizations under the same four-A100-40GB hardware envelope, pinned Qwen3-8B model, software stack, prompts, and arrival schedules. Our evaluation contains 150 audited conditions over short-chat, decode-heavy, and 32K prefill-heavy workloads. Four independent one-GPU replicas achieve the lowest end-to-end latency for short chat and long output and are the only architecture stable in every condition. Pipeline parallelism reduces 32K time to first token by 58-59% at non-stress rates, while hybrid pipeline-based disaggregation achieves the best 32K end-to-end latency at 0.4 requests/s. In contrast, B's single-VM static TP2+TP2 split, without independent phase scaling, does not improve tested latency over replication and collapses at higher 32K load. These results reveal a workload-architecture affinity: pipeline decomposition favors prefill-heavy computation, whereas replication favors decode-heavy and concurrent traffic. More broadly, decomposition is not a monotonic optimization; its value depends on matching parallelism granularity to the dominant phase and preserving queue stability.

Container scheduling.title: Examining QRMI as a Unified Interface for Quantum-HPC Integration
Container scheduling.summary: The efficient and scalable integration of quantum resources into high-performance computing (HPC) environments requires standardized mechanisms for resource management, scheduling, and workflow orchestration across diverse and heterogeneous infrastructures. The Quantum Resource Management Interface (QRMI) addresses this challenge through a thin, vendor-agnostic middleware layer that provides standardized APIs for scheduling, executing, and monitoring quantum workloads while exposing quantum resources as first-class schedulable resources alongside CPUs and GPUs. Although previous work demonstrated QRMI integration with the Slurm workload manager, its applicability across other workload managers remained unexamined. This paper extends the validation of QRMI to a broad range of workload managers, including PBS, LSF, Grid Engine, Kubernetes, and the Flux Framework, encompassing traditional batch schedulers, a cloud-native orchestration platform, and a graph-based scheduler. We examine the integration patterns, implementation requirements, and scheduler-specific considerations associated with each environment and compare QRMI with alternative approaches to quantum resource integration. We demonstrate that QRMI provides a portable and flexible abstraction layer that minimizes scheduler-specific modifications while enabling consistent access to heterogeneous quantum resources across both on-premises and cloud environments.
Container scheduling.comment: 12 pages, 3 tables, 1 figure, 3 listings, Published in the SC26 2nd International Workshop for Software Frameworks and Workload Management on Quantum-HPC Ecosystems (SFWM)

Container scheduling.title: Sensor Placement for Tsunami Early Warning via Large-Scale Bayesian Optimal Experimental Design
Container scheduling.summary: Real-time tsunami early warning relies on distributed sensor networks to infer seismic sources and seafloor motion. Optimizing these networks via Bayesian optimal experimental design (OED) is exceptionally challenging for systems governed by hyperbolic partial differential equations, which lack the spectral decay required by standard low-rank approximations. We present a scalable Bayesian OED framework for linear time-invariant systems. By reformulating the inverse problem in the data space, we transform OED into dense matrix subset selection. We propose a multi-GPU, Schur-complement-update-based, greedy algorithm that solves the OED problem using a pipelined approach that fully overlaps I/O with GPU computations. Our framework achieves near-perfect weak and strong scaling across hundreds of GPUs on Perlmutter and Frontier. Applied to the 2025 Gordon Bell Prize-winning digital twin for tsunami forecasting in the Cascadia Subduction Zone, we optimize a 175-sensor network, minimizing the uncertainty of a parameter field with over one billion degrees of freedom.

Container scheduling.title: Hyperion: Hierarchical Scheduling for Parallel LLM Acceleration in Multi-tier Networks
Container scheduling.summary: LLMs are increasingly executed at the edge, where limited GPU memory and heterogeneous computation jointly constrain deployment, which motivates model partitioning and request scheduling. In this setting, minimizing latency requires addressing the tight coupling between model placement and request scheduling across heterogeneous nodes, as suboptimal decisions in one domain can negate benefits in the other. In this paper, we propose Hyperion, a hierarchical two-stage framework that coordinates partitioning and scheduling for pipelined LLM inference. Hyperion reduces latency by balancing resources across tiers without requiring model retraining. Leveraging the timescale difference between partitioning and request arrivals, Stage 1 performs offline, inter-tier partitioning via a Hyperion Split with Dynamic Programming (HypSplit-DP) procedure to produce balanced stage times under tier capacity and memory constraints; to adapt to time-varying load, Stage 2 performs online, intra-tier scheduling with a lightweight Hyperion Scheduling for Real-Time (HypSched-RT) that maps each request to a feasible node using real-time estimates of queue length and effective capacity. Experiments with Llama 3 and Phi-3 demonstrate that Hyperion reduces latency by up to 46.9% (vs. GPipe) and 31.1% (vs. HEFT). Furthermore, Hyperion exhibits superior scalability for long-sequence generation, maintaining 25.5% lower latency and higher GPU utilization.

Container scheduling.title: When the Next Step Is Not One Step: Distribution-Aware Execution Modeling for Concurrent Go Programs
Container scheduling.summary: Predicting the next scheduler event of a concurrent program is ill-posed as single-label classification: repeated runs from the same trace prefix produce different, equally valid next events. We formulate next-event prediction for concurrent Go programs as estimating an empirical next-event distribution obtained from repeated executions, and release a benchmark with 945 training examples from hand-written and generated programs and 798 held-out predictions on 54 real-world GoKer bug kernels from systems such as CockroachDB, Kubernetes, gRPC and etcd. We fine-tune Qwen2.5-Coder-7B with low-rank adapters under a cross-entropy objective and a KL-to-empirical-distribution objective and compare them with zero-shot models and trivial baselines. The outcome is a neutral-to-negative result. The fine-tuned adapters (re-evaluated: 36.3% cross-entropy, 33.6% KL; originally reported 36.2% and 35.8%) are statistically indistinguishable from always predicting the majority event (35.5%), and an event n-gram model reaches 33-34%. Because each held-out prompt carries labels from about five runs, no deterministic predictor can exceed 58.9% top-1 accuracy, so we report macro-F1, balanced accuracy, per-class recall, program-clustered confidence intervals and binned calibration measured directly on both adapters. A sensitivity study with 100 runs per program shows that five-run targets are noisy (mean total-variation distance 0.24 from a 100-run reference), which plausibly limits what the KL objective can learn. Rare event types are essentially never predicted. A select-block goroutine-leak signature follows from scheduler semantics rather than learning. We release the data, adapters and tooling.
Container scheduling.comment: 15 pages, 5 figures. Accepted for poster presentation at ICTer 2026. Substantially revised evaluation with trivial baselines, adapter re-evaluation, corrected calibration analysis, and run-count sensitivity analysis; conclusions revised accordingly

Container scheduling.title: Federated style aware transformer aggregation of representations
Container scheduling.summary:
Personalized Federated Learning (PFL) faces persistent challenges, including domain heterogeneity from diverse client data, data imbalance due to skewed participation, and strict communication constraints. Traditional federated learning often lacks personalization, as a single global model cannot capture client-specific characteristics, leading to biased predictions and poor generalization, especially for clients with highly divergent data distributions.
  To address these issues, we propose FedSTAR, a style-aware federated learning framework that disentangles client-specific style factors from shared content representations. FedSTAR aggregates class-wise prototypes using a Transformer-based attention mechanism, allowing the server to adaptively weight client contributions while preserving personalization.
  Furthermore, by exchanging compact prototypes and style vectors instead of full model parameters, FedSTAR significantly reduces communication overhead. Experimental results demonstrate that combining content-style disentanglement with attention-driven prototype aggregation improves personalization and robustness in heterogeneous environments without increasing communication cost.
Container scheduling.comment: The authors have identified errors in the experimental setup and evaluation methodology that undermine the reliability of the reported results. Consequently, the experimental findings and conclusions of this paper cannot be considered valid. The authors have therefore decided to withdraw this manuscript

Container scheduling.title: HiPerfCC-KVCache: Accelerating Confidential LLM Serving with Hierarchical KV Caching
Container scheduling.summary: Hierarchical key-value (KV) caching reduces repeated prefill computation in large language model serving by retaining reusable state beyond GPU memory. Under GPU confidential computing (CC), however, protected transfers can erase this benefit. We show that bulk KV copies hold driver locks during prolonged CPU-side processing, stalling independent serving operations despite separate threads and streams. Our characterization on Hopper and Blackwell GPUs shows how lock scope, copy granularity, and allocation ownership affect foreground progress and transfer parallelism. Guided by these findings, we present HiPerfCC-KVCache, which manages resource lifetimes, prioritizes ready token readback between bounded backup submissions, and parallelizes KV restores through auxiliary contexts with shared GPU staging. Implemented in SGLang, HiPerfCC-KVCache uses existing protected transfer interfaces without hardware or driver changes. Across three models and three workloads on H200, HiPerfCC-KVCache achieves a geometric-mean output-token throughput speedup of $1.74\times$ (up to $2.72\times$) over the staged KV-transfer HiCache-Workers baseline at the highest tested loads. Mean time to first token decreases by 36% on average and up to 59%. The benefits generalize to RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell, with a geometric-mean throughput speedup of $1.28\times$ (up to $2.20\times$) over the same baseline. A capacity analysis further models and explains variation in gains and remaining gaps to CC-off serving.

Container scheduling.title: The Defect Is in the Arithmetic Between the Files: Static Detection of Exactly-Once Violations in Payment Pipelines
Container scheduling.summary: Whether a streaming payment pipeline charges a customer twice after a restart turns on a comparison nobody performs: how long the provider remembers an idempotency key, against how stale a record can be when the pipeline processes it for the second time. The first number is in the provider's documentation. The second is not written anywhere. It is assembled from a checkpoint interval in one file, a recovery assumption in a runbook, a restart delay in a third and a source's lateness bound in a fourth. Each file is defensible alone; the fault is in the relation between them. We give a checker that gathers those facts and states the relations, and a synthesiser that turns 335 of the 515 findings into a runnable scenario: these records, kill the job here, bring it back after this long, and this is the observable. 245 of them produce two charges. The central measurement is how far apart the evidence lies. Across a corpus of 630 pipelines we generated, 210 of them cannot be derived from fewer than three artifacts, and no single artifact yields more than 35 of the 305 duration findings. Executing the witnesses corrected our own rules: two were demoted after their scenarios produced a repeated call the provider's idempotency absorbed rather than a second charge. All 16 selected live witnesses reproduced their predicted observable against a real Kafka broker with a real process kill, and a matched control in which the provider never forgets the key did not, attributing the second charge to the key lifetime, not the replay. Fault injection finds the same defects only if the tester already assumed a long enough outage: one willing to simulate five minutes finds 15% of them, and 12 hours is needed for all. A sweep also locates a configuration with no application-level fix, where above a 14-minute recovery assumption the transaction timeout required to survive it exceeds the broker's own cap.

Checker, corpus generator, Docker configuration and every raw results file are at https://github.com/abhisheksharma2411/streamcheck (release v1.0.2); make reproduce rebuilds every figure, table and number in the paper from the raw results.
