Container scheduling.title: IndexerStage: Staging Indexer-K across Memory Tiers for Sparse-Attention LLM Serving
Container scheduling.summary:
Long-context sparse-attention serving can remain limited by graphics processing unit (GPU) memory after attention data is offloaded. DeepSeek Sparse Attention retains Indexer-K state to select the tokens that attention will read. Its indexer scans this growing state in full at every layer and decode step. A full scan requires the current layer's state, however, not simultaneous residency of every layer.
  We present IndexerStage, a serving runtime that externalizes Indexer-K state while preserving native GPU score, top-k, and attention kernels. It stages completed pages through shared execution buffers and preserves new entries locally. Joint memory-and-transfer admission checks storage and each layer's transfer demand before accepting a growing batch. The backing tier gathers pages; the model-serving GPU controls transfer timing and byte budgets.
  We implement IndexerStage in SGLang on 16 model-serving and 16 backing H800 GPUs. Across 16K--64K inputs, local streaming storage occupies 0.65--0.70 GiB per model-serving GPU. Relative to host-memory-backed HiSparse, batch size increases by 12.28--23.08% and decode throughput in tokens per second (TPS) reaches 1.08--1.14x. At 64K with the latent-KV backing path fixed, the larger batch achieves 1.10x decode TPS; enabling streaming at batch size 24 adds 2.42% to time per output token. Mixed-length dynamic serving increases mean generating batch size by 12.07% and delivers 1.31x decode TPS.

Container scheduling.title: TripleKV: Predict, Prefetch, Protect - KV Cache Management for AI Agents
Container scheduling.summary:
LLM agents alternate between inference and tool execution, repeatedly reusing their growing context across calls. Under high concurrency, their combined key-value (KV) cache working set can reach hundreds of GiB, far exceeding GPU memory capacity. As idle KV cache blocks are evicted to slower storage tiers, returning agents incur expensive retrievals that stall inference.
  To address this problem, we present TripleKV, a three-tier KV cache management system that hides the delays of these retrievals. In agentic workloads, the KV blocks needed by the next inference request are known in advance; only the time of their reuse is uncertain. TripleKV uses a tool-aware latency predictor to estimate when each tool call will complete and prefetches the required KV blocks from SSD into host DRAM ahead of time. Unlike GPU prefetching, this avoids reserving scarce GPU memory and interfering with concurrent inference requests. To further improve DRAM utilization, TripleKV eliminates duplication of GPU-resident blocks in DRAM, and introduces a victim-cache mechanism that refills blocks from SSD upon their eviction from GPU memory.
  Across data, web, and coding agents, TripleKV reduces the fraction of requests requiring critical-path SSD reads from 45-76% to under 10%. It also reduces P95 time to first token (TTFT) by up to 49% compared with vLLM extended with DRAM and SSD KV-cache tiers, and achieves 1.5-7$\times$ lower P95 TTFT than recent agent-aware systems.

Container scheduling.title: Making Repeated Variational Circuit Optimization Efficient on GPUs
Container scheduling.summary: Repeated numerical optimization is a defining workload for classical simulation of parameterized quantum circuits. Although successive training steps change gate parameters, they usually preserve circuit connectivity and reuse a small set of gate-layer patterns. We use this regularity to accelerate gradient evaluation on GPUs. Our framework combines execution primitives for common circuit layers with adjoint differentiation, coordinating state evolution and derivative computation to reduce launch overhead, intermediate storage, and state-vector traffic. Because effective schedules depend on circuit size, gate structure, and device resources, our framework retains several execution choices instead of committing to a single schedule. Structural and hardware constraints narrow these choices, after which measurements on representative layers guide plan selection. The selected plans are reused while circuit structure remains fixed, spreading the selection cost over repeated training iterations. This approach targets the computation required by optimization rather than forward simulation alone, while retaining the numerical semantics of state-vector differentiation. Experiments across multiple circuit families and GPU platforms compare our framework with the native GPU adjoint implementation in PennyLane Lightning. The results demonstrate substantially lower gradient evaluation times over the evaluated workloads, together with the numerical accuracy checks reported in the evaluation.

Container scheduling.title: CCAMoE: Cache-Conditioned Adaptive Inference for Offloaded MoE
Container scheduling.summary: Expert offloading enables Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) inference on memory-constrained GPUs, but expert transfers and CPU execution limit decoding performance. Speculative decoding can mitigate these costs, yet separate draft weights consume scarce GPU memory and longer drafts increase verification demand. In this paper, we present CCAMoE, a unified runtime that coordinates adaptive speculative decoding with concurrent expert-cache updates. Its design has three key features: 1) Cache-only drafting, which reuses resident target experts to generate proposals and routing hints without separate draft weights; 2) Draft-guided cache updates, which anticipate expert demand and overlap transfers with computation to support subsequent drafting and verification; and 3) Cost-aware draft-length control, which balances expected acceptance against execution cost. Together, these mechanisms coordinate proposal generation and cache preparation through a shared evolving cache, improving proposal quality while reducing verification cost. Across various MoE models, GPU platforms, and workloads, CCAMoE consistently achieves the lowest decoding latency, with up to 2.33$\times$ speedup over state-of-the-art baselines.

Container scheduling.title: DisSparse: Pipelined Top-$p$ Sparse Attention for Long-Context LLM Serving
Container scheduling.summary: Long-context LLM inference is bottlenecked by the memory demands of the key-value (KV) cache, whose size scales linearly with context length. Dynamic sparse attention reduces this bottleneck by fetching and attending only to a critical subset of tokens. The dominant primitive in dynamic sparse attention research and deployment is fixed-budget top-$k$ selection, which is favored because its deterministic block count aligns with the static memory allocation that systems like vLLM rely on. Top-$k$ uses a fixed budget regardless of how attention mass is distributed across heads, layers, and decode steps, leading to either wasted bandwidth on heads with peaky attention or dropped context on heads with diffuse attention. Top-$p$ (nucleus) selection adapts naturally to this variation but has seen limited adoption in production serving systems due to two system-level challenges: variable block counts that break deterministic block allocation and computationally expensive selection kernels that exceed the cost of attention itself. We present DisSparse, a serving system that integrates top-$p$ sparse attention into vLLM end-to-end. DisSparse decouples block selection from the scheduler's critical path, hides selection latency behind layer computation via a two-stream pipeline, and introduces a single-pass histogram-based top-$p$ kernel. We further observe intra-block sparsity, the inflation of selection budgets caused by mixing high- and low-importance tokens within fixed-size KV cache blocks, and address it with a token relocation kernel guided by accumulated prefill attention scores. Across long- and medium-context benchmarks on multiple models, DisSparse achieves 1.17x to 1.80x speedup in sparsity analysis (block selection) over state-of-the-art top-$p$ methods with negligible accuracy loss and supports up to 8x larger maximum batch sizes than dense vLLM under the same memory budget.

Container scheduling.title: Personalized Execution Time Optimization for Billion-Scale Scheduled Jobs
Container scheduling.summary: Scheduled batch jobs are widely used on asynchronous computing platforms to execute enterprise applications such as promotional notifications and candidate pre-computation for recommender systems. Delivering or updating information at the right time is important for user experience and execution impact, yet providing a versatile, personalized execution time optimization solution across diverse product scenarios while maintaining reasonable infrastructure costs remains challenging. In this paper, we present a deployed system that serves billions of users daily, combining learning-to-rank with a "best time policy" for execution time selection. We describe the four-stage evolution of our approach: from heuristic peak-hour rules, to pointwise ML-based activity pattern predictions, to a linear signal assembler with globally fixed weights, and finally to a contextual ensemble learner that produces per-user adaptive fusion weights via a neural policy network trained with listwise learning-to-rank objectives. We further report the discovery of cross-use-case cannibalization effects and introduce a coordination system to mitigate the problem. Our production experiments demonstrate measurable improvements in both execution efficiency and downstream product impact. We share deployment lessons including failure analyses and design decisions accumulated over four years of operating this system at scale. To our knowledge, this represents the first ML-based multi-tenant execution time optimization system deployed across different product domains at industrial scale.
Container scheduling.comment: In 39th Annual Conference on Innovative Applications of Artificial Intelligence, February 18-20, 2027

Container scheduling.title: GDNShift: Live Migration and Joint State Scheduling for Gated DeltaNet Inference
Container scheduling.summary: Live migration of a streaming Gated DeltaNet (GDN) request requires rebuilding its recurrent state at the correct token boundary on a replica with identical weights. We propose a cross-replica recovery protocol based on compact update logs and implement and numerically validate exact catch-up. Compact logs stream a base state and ordered updates while the source continues decoding. Exact catch-up uses native single-token decode and releases the source once the destination has what it needs to continue independently. Across 120 complete pure-GDN configurations on three dual-GPU deployments, compact logs reduced the mean exact handoff gap from 790.8 to 149.5 ms relative to a background snapshot. Exact catch-up reduced mean source release time from 818.0 to 42.7 ms. In a prospective cross-host evaluation with relaxed arithmetic, a sealed selector chose the minimum-gap path in 39 of 40 configurations and reduced mean gap by 2.17% over a frozen network lookup. In nine whole-request migration paths for hybrid Qwen3.5-0.8B, the KV transfer ranking changed with the GDN path in 51 of 90 configurations. Per-configuration hindsight selection among the evaluated exact paths reduced mean gap by 34.7% over the best measured KV transfer paired with a GDN snapshot. In a separate held-out replay on 30 configurations, a locally calibrated selector reduced the exact gap by 15.4% over frozen network lookup.
Container scheduling.comment: 9 pages, 3 figures, 6 tables. Adds a third pure-GDN deployment, prospective path selection, and a nine-path hybrid-model comparison

Container scheduling.title: Adaptive Warm-State Retention for Serverless Cold-Start Mitigation: Treating Keep-Alive Time as an Online Control Parameter
Container scheduling.summary: Serverless platforms are easy to operate but pay a recurring price in cold starts: when a function is called after sitting idle, its execution environment must be rebuilt before the request can run, and latency suffers. The usual fix keeps idle environments alive for a fixed window, but a single value rarely fits a changing workload: too high wastes idle capacity, too low causes avoidable cold starts. We argue the keep-alive window should not be a fixed deployment constant; instead we treat it as a per-function runtime parameter, adjusted online from what the system observes, kept separate from how many replicas to run. We build an external retention controller for OpenFaaS/faasd that needs no platform changes, driven by two simple agents: a reactive AIMD (Additive-Increase Multiplicative-Decrease) rule and a UCB1 multi-armed bandit. Against fixed-timeout baselines and a predictive histogram keep-alive, on steady, bursty, and trace-derived workloads (Huawei Serverless 2023), the bandit cuts the aggregate cold-start rate from 63% under immediate scale-to-zero to 3%, holds P95 tail latency at the level of the longest-retention fixed baseline, and uses about 13% less accumulated warm time than that baseline, while also beating the predictive baseline. No fixed timeout is best on every metric, whereas the adaptive agents reach a favorable operating point without manual tuning; on the bursty workload at a converged horizon the bandit's advantage is statistically significant. On a multi-node Kubernetes cluster under the platform's own Horizontal Pod Autoscaler, the controller coexists with an autoscaler it does not control: the replica count follows load identically across policies, and retention independently governs warm time.

Container scheduling.title: Practical activation sparsity for quantized LLMs on personal devices
Container scheduling.summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly run on personal devices, where generating text is slow: producing each token requires reading all of the model's weights from memory. Two techniques reduce this memory traffic. Quantization stores the weights in 4 to 8 bits. Activation sparsity treats near-zero activations as zero and skips the weights they multiply; prior work shows that it skips 40-50% of the weights of modern LLMs without retraining, at little loss in accuracy, also on quantized models. Yet the two do not combine in execution: a quantization format packs the weights that multiply many consecutive activations into one block, and a block can be skipped only if all of these activations are near zero, which rarely happens. Moreover, the near-zero activations change with every token, so balancing the GPU's load and finding them add run-time overhead. We present SpQt, which makes activation sparsity practical for quantized LLMs. SpQt (1) stores each activation's quantized weights contiguously, in a zigzag layout that keeps the quantization formats unchanged; (2) divides the nonzero activations evenly among groups of GPU threads, so the load stays balanced; and (3) finds the nonzero activations inside kernels that each decode step already runs before its matrix products, such as normalization, so that finding them adds no kernel launch. Built into llama.cpp and tested on five devices from a phone to a desktop, with Apple and NVIDIA GPUs and four quantization formats, SpQt generates tokens 1.45-2.15x faster than llama.cpp at 50% sparsity, with up to 2.6x less energy per token. With SpQt, a device can choose a sparsity level in addition to a quantization format, trading a small loss in accuracy for speed and energy.
Container scheduling.comment: 14 pages, 13 figures, 3 tables. v2: substantially revised, with a new title and an extended evaluation on five devices with Apple and NVIDIA GPUs and four quantization formats

Container scheduling.title: Discrete Incremental Voting: New Bounds for General Graphs and Expanders
Container scheduling.summary:
We analyze the discrete incremental voting process (DIV) introduced by Cooper, Radzik, and Shiraga [OPODIS '23]. In this process, we consider a set $V$ of $n$ nodes connected in an undirected graph $G = (V, E)$ where each node has an integer opinion. In one step a randomly selected node interacts with its randomly selected neighbor and changes its opinion by $1$ in the direction of the neighbour's opinion. The process converges to a unique opinion that, in expectation, is the degree-weighted average of the initial opinions.
  We show that if the graph has conductance $Φ(G)$, the ratio of the average to smallest degree is $γ(G)$, and the maximal difference between initial opinions is $K$, then the expected convergence time is ${O}\left({n\left(K\log (Kn)+γ(G) n \right)}/{Φ(G)^2}\right)$. This bound is essentially optimal for a large class of graphs of bounded expansion. We also show that for regular graphs, if the second largest eigenvalue is $o(1/\log^4 n)$ and $K$ is $o\left({n}/{\log^2 n}\right)$, then w.h.p.\ DIV converges to the initial average opinion (rounded up or down).
Container scheduling.comment: Fixed typo in the abstract and minor improvements

Container scheduling.title: Weave: Routing-Adaptive Runtime Warp Scheduling for MoE Megakernels
Container scheduling.summary: The Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture is widely used in mainstream large language models. Under expert parallelism (EP), state-of-the-art systems fuse each MoE layer into a persistent megakernel for high performance. By the nature of EP, each GPU's communication and computation volumes vary with the routing result. However, prior work either fixes how GPU resources are divided between communication and computation at compile time (e.g., MegaMoE), or adapts to runtime dynamism only at coarse-grained SM granularity (e.g., mKernel), dedicating whole SMs to communication and leaving their Tensor Cores idle. At the finer warp granularity within each SM, static warp schedules can neither match routing-dependent loads nor prevent warps from idling while waiting for inputs or after finishing their assigned work. Therefore, we propose Weave, an MoE megakernel with three key designs. First, a spatial schedule allocates resources between communication and computation at both SM and warp granularities to match each GPU's load. Second, a temporal schedule switches warp roles as execution progresses, enlisting all warps at the start and end of a layer and selectively handing output scatter to idle communication warps. Third, a fused cost model jointly selects both schedules per GPU at launch from runtime routing statistics. Across all evaluated platforms, Weave outperforms the strongest baselines: under EP8 over DeepGEMM-MegaMoE, it speeds up the MoE layer by 1.30x geomean and up to 1.97x on SM103, and by 1.24x geomean and up to 1.72x on SM90; under EP16 on CDNA3, it beats the fastest official RCCL+AITER baseline by 1.44x geomean (up to 2.87x; 1.67x over vLLM).

Container scheduling.title: Learning in Symbiosis: Heterogeneous Federated Learning with ANNs and SNNs
Container scheduling.summary: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs), widely regarded as the third generation of neural networks, represent a promising neuromorphic computing paradigm with the potential to reduce the energy footprint of Artificial Intelligence (AI). Their en-ergy efficiency makes SNNs particularly attractive for resource-constrained Edge AI devices, motivating growing research interest in Federated Learning (FL) with SNNs. Despite these advantages, integrating SNNs into existing FL systems remains challenging, as replacing all conventional Artificial Neural Network (ANN) devices with SNN-based alternatives is impractical. Instead, we envision a gradual transition toward neuromorphic Edge AI, where ANN and SNN devices coexist and collaboratively participate in FL. To facilitate this transition, we propose Hybrid Neuromorphic Federated Learning (HNFL), a framework that enables joint training of heterogeneous ANN and SNN devices within an FL environment. Through experiments on CIFAR-10 using both VGG9 and ResNet architectures, we demonstrate the mutual benefits of collaborative ANN-SNN training. Specifically, HNFL achieves an average improvement of 16.85% when incorporating SNN devices into ANN-based FL and 8.02% when incorporating ANN devices into SNN-based FL. Furthermore, HNFL produces sparser spiking activity in the trained SNN models, with reductions of 12.4% for SResNet and 22.4% for SVGG9. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to demonstrate that ANNs and SNNs can coexist and mutually benefit from collaborative training in FL, providing a practical path toward the gradual integration of neuromorphic computing into existing Edge AI systems.
Container scheduling.comment: Manuscript submitted to: IEEE International Conference on Communications (ICC) 2027. 6 pages, 3 figures, 1 table, 1 pseudo code

Container scheduling.title: Asynchronous Byzantine Lattice Agreement with Logarithmic Response Time and Optimal Resilience
Container scheduling.summary:
Lattice agreement is a fundamental coordination primitive in which processes decide on comparable values rather than identical ones. In the asynchronous message-passing setting with Byzantine failures, existing algorithms either require authentication or do not simultaneously achieve optimal resilience and logarithmic response time.
  We present an asynchronous Byzantine lattice agreement algorithm that tolerates up to $f$ Byzantine failures among $n>3f$ processes, requires no authentication, and completes in $O(\log f)$ time. The algorithm builds on the classifier-tree framework of Attiya and Rachman, replacing shared-memory communication with quorum-based message passing.
  The main challenge is preserving the information-flow invariants underlying the classifier tree despite Byzantine behavior. To address this challenge, we introduce Supported Reliable Broadcast (SRB), a communication abstraction that combines reliable broadcast with protocol-specific admissibility checks. Messages are disseminated using reliable broadcast, but are delivered to the protocol only after verifying that they are consistent with previously propagated information about the sender's state. This prevents Byzantine processes from bypassing the information-flow guarantees required by the classifier tree.
  A central technical difficulty lies in breaking the apparent circular dependency between message delivery and admissibility: admissibility depends on local state established by previously delivered messages, while message delivery itself depends on admissibility. Our proof resolves this circularity by separating reliable dissemination from admissibility propagation, yielding a modular correctness argument.

Container scheduling.title: IsoMoE: Placement-Invariant Hybrid CPU-GPU MoE Inference with Lossless 12-bit Experts
Container scheduling.summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models scale model capacity at low computational cost. Hybrid CPU-GPU inference offloads some experts to the CPU, enabling a single GPU to run MoE models larger than its memory. Expert placement changes with free GPU memory and should only affect speed. However, the greedy decoding outputs of existing hybrid engines change with placement. This is because the two devices use different arithmetic to compute experts. In addition, decoding is limited by CPU memory bandwidth. Lossless compression reduces memory traffic, but the CPU decompresses entropy-coded formats too slowly to keep up with memory reads. To address these challenges, we propose IsoMoE, an efficient hybrid MoE inference system that guarantees that its outputs do not change with expert placement. IsoMoE introduces (i) a GPU expert kernel that bitwise replays the arithmetic of the CPU expert kernel, (ii) a memory layout that allows the CPU to efficiently compute lossless 12-bit experts using AVX-512 dot-product instructions, and (iii) a dual micro-batch pipeline that overlaps CPU and GPU computation without changing the outputs. Experimental results on three MoE models show that IsoMoE produces bitwise identical outputs across different expert placements. It is also faster than the fastest baseline in every setting, achieving an average decoding speedup of 1.26$\times$ and a maximum speedup of 1.54$\times$. Our source code is publicly available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/isomoe-artifact-9C21/.

Container scheduling.title: Isonomy: Isolating Every Request from Timing Side Channels at Nearly Full-Sharing Throughput in Multi-Instance LLM Prefill
Container scheduling.summary: Many long prompts share a prefix, and reusing its cached keys and values saves prefill computation. A cache hit, however, makes the first token arrive earlier and can reveal that another request used the same prefix, so providers share the cache only within an account. Under least privilege, even permission to send and pay for requests should not expose other requests' prompts in the same account. This matters because agents send unreviewed requests carrying private data, resellers pool users behind one account, and creden-tials can be stolen. Isonomy therefore isolates each request by default and lets requests opt into explicit sharing groups. Rather than give up reuse, it keeps one cache shared across accounts and hides only hits on prefixes cached outside a request's group. We target deployments where clients cannot observe one another's load, because there it suffices to hide these hits in the request's own timing. On three commercial APIs, our listeners could not distinguish added prefill work from a short request beyond measurement noise. Built on vLLM, Isonomy's gateway applies the deployment's routing rule to load and visible cache entries only, which yields the instance where the request would run if hidden hits missed. On that instance, the prediction mode estimates when the first token would be ready from the queue and the visible prefix, and gates its release. The execution mode instead reserves the work a hidden hit skips and fills it with other requests' prompts where possible. In direct-probe tests on two, four, and eight instances with every request isolated, both modes kept the upper bound on a probe's advantage within measure-ment noise at both prefix lengths. At saturation, the prediction mode retains 0.98 of unprotected sharing's throughput on two workloads with account labels, whereas isolation by account retains 0.95, or 0.80 where more reuse crosses accounts.

Container scheduling.title: Omakase: Execution Congestion Control through Conflict-Graph Integration in Multi-Proposer Blockchain
Container scheduling.summary:
As multi-proposer protocols push consensus throughput, transaction execution has become the dominant bottleneck in blockchains. Layer-1 blockchains parallelize execution either pessimistically (Solana, Sui), requiring upfront state-access declarations and serializing contended transactions, or optimistically (Aptos, Sei, Monad), resolving dependencies at run time but suffering cascading aborts under contention. Both treat blocks in isolation, leaving inter-block parallelism unexploited and most cores idle.
  We introduce Omakase, a parallel execution framework that combines pre-execution, inter-block conflict-graph integration, and graph-aware Optimistic Concurrency Control (OCC). Replicas use idle cores to pre-execute only the blocks they propose, spreading prediction work across concurrent proposers. After building per-block conflict graphs and identifying their hot resources, a greedy scheduler integrates graphs across the blocks committed in a round, keeping an integration only when a lightweight balance heuristic predicts a parallelism gain. A graph-aware OCC executor then runs the integrated graph, admitting transactions in dependency order, which eliminates aborts when the predicted graph is exact and reduces re-executions when it is not.
  On 15,000 Ethereum mainnet blocks (~2.4M transactions) and synthetic workloads with configurable contention, Omakase reaches a 2.47x speedup over sequential execution, well above single-block OCC and graph-aware baselines. Against the strongest alternative, which runs the whole round as one optimistic window, Omakase matches mean throughput but is markedly more stable under high contention, because integration bounds how much optimistic work is in flight: this is the congestion control of our title. Integration is not free, but overlapping it with execution across rounds hides 94% of its measured cost in the validator pipeline.

Container scheduling.title: Dugong: Composing Uncertified DAG Consensus
Container scheduling.summary: There is a significant number of uncertified DAG consensus protocols spanning partial synchrony and asynchrony as well as crash, Byzantine, and hybrid fault models, yet each protocol is designed, proved, and implemented from scratch. We introduce Dugong, a single parameterized protocol that unifies uncertified DAG consensus protocols. Its core algorithm, the Decider can implement eight existing protocols and yields four new ones by just tuning its parameters. Given the property that DAGs decouple throughput from latency Dugong presents a simple trade-off between latency and resilience to network and node faults. An operator can adapt the parameters of their protocol epoch-by-epoch to adjust the resilience without needing to develop a new protocol or worry about throughput. Around the Decider, Dugong layers production feature mechanisms (adaptive leader scheduling, checkpoints, responsive liveness, and crash recovery) that provably compose with each other and with the Decider's configurations. We formalize Dugong in Lean 4, proving safety and liveness under the established definitions of Byzantine atomic broadcast, and identify and repair gaps in published proofs. Finally, we implement Dugong as a reusable Rust library paired with a discrete-event network simulator, enabling direct latency comparisons across network and fault models.

Container scheduling.title: Improved (Minimum) Spanning Tree Construction in the HYBRID Model
Container scheduling.summary: In the HYBRID$_0$ model, vertices exchange $O(\log n)$-bit messages in synchronous rounds, both along input edges (local communication) and directly to vertices whose IDs they know (global communication). The local capacity is the maximum number of messages a vertex may send per round to each input neighbor, and the global capacity is the maximum number of global messages it may send, and also receive, per round. The standard capacity is local capacity $O(1)$ and global capacity $O(\log n)$. A well-formed tree (WFT) is a virtual tree of maximum degree $O(1)$ and diameter $O(\log n)$. Known algorithms construct a spanning tree (ST) and a WFT either in $O(\log n)$ rounds with global capacity $O(\log^2 n)$ or with standard capacity in $O(\log^2 n)$ rounds. We give a randomized algorithm that constructs an ST and a WFT in every connected component of any graph in $O(\log n)$ rounds with high probability under standard capacity. Our approach is based on a $Δ$-pseudo-spanning representation ($Δ$-PSR): a virtual network of maximum degree $Δ$ with restoration information, such that any spanning tree of this network can be restored to a spanning tree of the input graph in $O(\log n)$ rounds. The algorithm of Götte et al. can be viewed as constructing an $O(\log n)$-PSR, which accounts for its global capacity $O(\log^2 n)$. Our main contribution is to construct an $O(1)$-PSR in $O(\log n)$ rounds with standard capacity. As applications, for $k$ distinct edge weights and any integer $1\le p\le k$, we construct an exact minimum spanning tree in $O((k/p)\log n)$ rounds with local capacity $O(p)$ and global capacity $O(p\log n)$, and the same tradeoff applies to $(1+ε)$-approximate minimum spanning trees. We also compute biconnected components, articulation points, and bridges in $O(\log n)$ rounds with standard capacity, down from the previous global capacity $O(\log^5 n)$.
Container scheduling.comment: 26 pages, 3 figures, 1 table. Full version of a paper to appear at OPODIS 2026

Container scheduling.title: AscendGYM: A Cost-Aware Kernel Optimization Benchmark for Real-World Workloads on Ascend NPUs
Container scheduling.summary: Kernel optimization is essential for efficient large language model (LLM) training and inference on Ascend NPUs. Existing Ascend kernel benchmarks primarily focus on kernel generation, with less emphasis on the ability of agents to optimize existing implementations under input configurations drawn from real workloads. To address this requirement, we introduce AscendGYM, a benchmark whose initial suite comprises 48 kernels across three difficulty levels. Each kernel is paired with test cases whose data types and tensor shapes are collected from real-world training and inference tasks. Consequently, performance improvements on AscendGYM map directly to the corresponding workloads. In terms of usability, two evaluation modes are supported in AscendGYM: model evaluation and model-harness evaluation. The kernel optimization capabilities of both trained models and custom agents are allowed to be measured. It provides a complete execution environment that closely reproduces how Ascend kernels are invoked in practical pipelines. For model evaluation, it additionally includes a built-in harness equipped with search orchestration and experience accumulation. Finally, we propose a new metric, the Speedup-Token Score (STS), which quantifies performance gains relative to token cost. By jointly considering speedup and cost, STS enables the assessment of practical kernel optimization capability of a model or harness under an acceptable budget. AscendGYM is available at https://github.com/SLAI-AITP/AscendGYM.
Container scheduling.comment: 20 pages, 12 figures, 2 tables. Technical Report. Code available at https://github.com/SLAI-AITP/AscendGYM

Container scheduling.title: Drive Failure and Lifetime Simulation in the Backblaze Drive Statistics Corpus, 2013-2026
Container scheduling.summary:
Storage simulators estimate data-loss risk from assumptions about drive lifetimes and dependence between failures. We test these assumptions against Backblaze's daily records from April 2013 to June 2026: 504,624 data drives with usable power-on ages, 99 drive models, 2.0 million drive-years and 31,881 recorded failures, including removals of drives judged likely to fail. We test failure-count forecasts over nine successive years and forecast the drives already in service at each prediction date.
  Accounting for drive-model differences and attributes improves the score assigned to observed failure counts about 4.3 times as much as replacing a single Weibull with two competing Weibulls under the same drive-model treatment. Fleet failure risk falls early and rises at older ages, but the fixed bathtub benchmark predicts 2.4 times the observed failures. Across 169 well-observed drive-model years selected using earlier records, 95% prediction intervals cover 44% of observed counts without annual variation and 92% with fleet-wide changes and shared good or bad years for each drive model.
  For drives already in service, a SMART warning raises one-year failure-risk ranking AUC from 0.64 to 0.73. Boosted trees using monthly SMART records give the best individual probability forecasts, yet predict 19% too many failures at one year and 22% too many at 90 days. Long-term survival depends on how aging is separated from calendar time: fitted fifteen-year survival probabilities differ by up to 18 percentage points, and assumptions about future calendar trends by up to 27 points. We provide samplers for storage simulations that represent drive-model differences, shared risks, and changes in drive condition.
Container scheduling.comment: 174 pages. Sustainable Systems Laboratory Technical Report SSL-TR-2026-001, Preprint v0.1

Container scheduling.title: CTRL: Concurrent Training and Rollout for LLM Reinforcement Learning via GPU Co-Residency
Container scheduling.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training of large language models runs two GPU workloads with different hardware demands: rollout decoding, which is dominated by memory access and whose batch shrinks as responses finish, and a dense learner. Current systems either time-share every GPU between them, paying serial phases and switches, or split GPUs into pools whose sizes change only in whole devices. We present CTRL, which makes co-residency a third RL execution layout: every GPU runs a learner rank beside a persistent rollout engine, sharing the device under CUDA MPS. A host-owned learner makes the layout fit: optimizer state stays in host memory, and policy weights stream layer by layer through a bounded GPU window. A publication gate trains each ready batch first and waits only before releasing the next policy, keeping a dropless staleness bound. A step-time bound guides compute-share selection, and a GPU-time ledger explains overlap and sharing costs. On H100, A800, and RTX 4090 GPUs with Qwen3 models, CTRL achieves 1.11-2.24$\times$ the throughput of the stronger of verl's asynchronous baselines across 24 workload settings with the staleness limit set to two, and 1.23$\times$ verl's colocate_async on eight H100 GPUs. With the same learner, co-residency is 1.10-1.26$\times$ faster than time-sharing on all three platforms and 1.10-1.30$\times$ faster than the best measured whole-GPU split on H100 DAPO-Math workloads at 256-528 trajectories per step, on four and eight GPUs.

Container scheduling.title: Selective Verification in Multi-Agent Orchestration with Large Language Models
Container scheduling.summary: Agents can agree because they relied on the same flawed evidence. We use an exact model of nine binary votes to examine when a verifier should intervene. In the main comparison, workers err 20 percent of the time under ordinary conditions, shared failures occur in 10 percent of cases, and the verifier errs 2 percent of the time in either state. When worker error during a shared failure is 80 percent, checking close votes yields 7.93 percent verdict error, compared with 9.06 percent for random checks at the same expected check rate. The ordering reverses at 90 percent worker error during failure. At the matched check rate for that regime, checking close votes yields 9.98 percent error, random checks yield 9.41 percent, and ranking checks by their expected error reduction yields 6.73 percent. The model also shows that passing branch vote counts preserves the flat majority and reduces the number of messages the root receives. A design guide and a documentation audit of four Python frameworks translate these findings into implementation choices.

Container scheduling.title: Flying over The Uncertain Nature (FORTUNE): Intelligent and Humanistic 3D Path Planning for Low-Altitude Collaboration
Container scheduling.summary: Low-altitude intelligent agents are driving demand for timely, socially responsible collaborative sensing in dynamic urban environments. Yet jointly handling heterogeneous spatio-temporal sensing demands, real-time uncertainty, and human-centered constraints in a unified multi-uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV) framework remains challenging. We study 3D multi-UAV path planning and joint task assignment under heterogeneous spatio-temporal uncertainty of ground points of interest (PoIs). Unlike studies assuming static, known PoIs, we formulate a unified model capturing persistent (Type-I), temporally predictable (Type-II), and emergent unpredictable (Type-III) demands. Following the low-altitude-for-good principle, we explicitly model altitude-dependent societal and environmental costs, including noise and public safety risks, jointly optimizing sensing effectiveness and socially compliant operations. To solve the resulting large-scale mixed-integer nonlinear problem, we propose FORTUNE, a hierarchical offline-online framework. Offline, a Transformer-based predictor forecasts Type-II activation windows, while an enhanced sparrow search algorithm (ES2A) with priority-aware decoding and danger-aware evolution generates globally coordinated flight plans. Online, lightweight trajectory refinement accommodates new Type-III PoIs while preserving global mission coherence. Experiments on real-world traffic and synthetic datasets show FORTUNE consistently outperforms state-of-the-art benchmarks, validating effectiveness, scalability, and practical applicability in dynamic low-altitude systems.

Container scheduling.title: PLoQ: A Prompt-Specific Low-Rank Basis for 4-bit Quantization of LLM Activations
Container scheduling.summary: Low-bit activation quantization of large language models remains challenging, as a small number of dominant directions dictate the quantization range. State-of-the-art methods isolate these directions in a high-precision subspace through transformations calibrated offline and folded into the weights, which fixes the subspace for all prompts, leaving each prompt's few unique directions unprotected, and rules it out wherever no weight can absorb the transformation. We present PLoQ, a prompt-adaptive low-rank decomposition that extracts the dominant activation components before quantization, quantizes them separately, and restores them within the layer's GEMM, without modifying the weights. The low-rank component's basis is estimated from each prompt during prefill and reused throughout decoding. At the same bit width as state-of-the-art mixed-precision quantization (4-bit weights, activations and K/V cache with an eighth of the channels at 8 bits, about 4.2 bits per activation on average), PLoQ outperforms it on all six Llama and Qwen models from 1B to 70B parameters, at up to 8k tokens (16k on two of them), recovering up to 46% of the perplexity that the state of the art still loses to 4-bit activations. On Llama-3.1-8B at 8k tokens it adds only 4% to prefill and 8% to decoding.

Container scheduling.title: Adaptive Determinantal Client Scheduling in Federated Learning
Container scheduling.summary: Scheduling clients for model training is critical in federated learning due to both data and system heterogeneity. Most previous works focus on the quality of the scheduled clients to achieve faster convergence, shorter wall-clock convergence time, or better average model performance. They rarely consider the diversity of clients, which is important to counter heterogeneity and improve performance for the worst-off clients. In this work, we advocate the use of determinantal point processes (DPPs) to model and enhance the diversity in client scheduling. We first design the kernel matrices of DPPs using gradient information and quality scores, which inherently enables a flexible quality-diversity trade-off. Applying fast MAP inference over DPPs, we propose Adaptive Determinantal Client Scheduling (ADCS) in FL. We further quantify the gradient approximation error of ADCS and develop convergence analysis for general biased client selection in FL with non-convex loss functions. We conduct comparative numerical experiments showing that ADCS outperforms state-of-the-art client scheduling algorithms, including both quality-based and diversity-based ones.

Container scheduling.title: Contexture: Runtime Context Eviction for High-Throughput Agent Serving
Container scheduling.summary:
LLM agents such as Hermes, OpenClaw, and Codex repeatedly resend growing execution histories, increasing shared GPU key-value (KV) cache demand in high-bandwidth memory (HBM). We show that shared KV capacity limits agent-serving throughput. Existing context-reduction methods lack global cache-state visibility, while runtime KV managers lack tool-execution information. Tracing tokens to their originating tool operations reveals that later operations supersede earlier outputs and associated turns, identifying 64% of recorded final-history tokens as removal candidates.
  We present Contexture, a harness- and model-agnostic architecture for runtime context eviction. Contexture separates the harness's full conversation history from the model's execution context, reducing subsequent requests' KV demand without modifying harness logic or model execution. It combines tool-execution information with global visibility into shared KV pressure and prefix residency: supersession identifies removal candidates, while runtime state determines when removal justifies sacrificing cached computation. This coordination reduces memory demand and decode KV traffic while limiting re-prefill interference with concurrent decoding, without additional model calls or training. Across two models, two harnesses, and two benchmarks, Contexture improves throughput under SLO by 20-73% over the best of no eviction, harness compaction, AgentDiet, and Continuum, and by 7-63% over observation masking in five of eight configurations, and reduces GPU energy per completed session by up to 11%. It also raises throughput under SLO by 23% over LMCache alone on H100. Live-agent experiments show a mean accuracy improvement of 1.4 percentage points over unloaded no eviction, with a worst-case loss of 3.7 points, while observation masking loses 3-28 points.

Container scheduling.title: Analysis of Multi-Client Inference Techniques for Vision-Language-Action Models
Container scheduling.summary: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) are a new class of machine learning model for generalizable robot control. While they enable robots to perform complex tasks in unseen environments, serving VLAs leaves hardware idle between inference passes and under-utilized during inference. Serving multiple clients at once can improve utilization, but fundamental multi-client techniques such as batching and co-execution have not been characterized for VLAs. We therefore characterize the trade-offs these known techniques impose across latency, throughput, power, and hardware utilization. Our findings inform trade-offs and challenges for future multi-VLA serving systems.

Container scheduling.title: Joint SLA Admission and Risk Allocation for Cloud Resource Provisioning
Container scheduling.summary: Cloud controllers must reserve enough CPU and memory to meet demand without leaving too much capacity idle. Under a shared service-level agreement (SLA), a shortage of CPU or memory (considered as resource) counts toward the same limit. Dividing the allowed shortage risk between them changes how much extra capacity each need. We study this choice when forecast-error histories are short or correlated over time. Our controller compares different approaches to split the allowed shortage risk between resources. For each split, the controller uses historical forecast errors to determine how much extra capacity to reserve. It checks whether the history is enough to support that split and its consistency across different parts of the history. Among the splits that pass, it chooses the one with the lowest combined cost of shortages and idle capacity. Otherwise, the controller continues serving the workload with a calibrated fallback. In our simulation, we set a joint SLA target of sufficient CPU and memory in at least 95% of time slots and used 192 hours of historical forecast errors to structure the controller. Compared with always using fallback, the controller reduced the time slots allocation with either of the resource shortage by 1.04 percentage points on average. This reduction came with a 0.0091 increase in normalized cost from shortages and idle capacity. In the Bitbrains trace, five nonoverlapping test windows did not provide clear evidence of whether shortages increased or decreased. We also examine how execution delays and adjustment limits affect this trade off.
